title: Indiana governor is urged to let death sentence proceed against man who killed 2 kids in fire
summary: The Indiana Parole Board is recommending that the death penalty remain in place for a man who killed two children in a house fire
story: The Indiana Parole Board is recommending that the death penalty remain in place for a man who killed two children in a house fire

A death sentence for an Indiana man who killed his girlfriend’s two children in a house fire should remain in place, the state parole board recommended Wednesday, just days before a Nov. 5 execution by lethal injection.
Jeffrey Weisheit has a right under Indiana law to seek clemency and ask for a life sentence for his murder and arson convictions. The final decision rests with Gov. Mike Braun.
“We unanimously recommend that you deny Jeffrey Weisheit's request,” parole board chairperson Gwendolyn Horth wrote to Braun.

The board heard two days of testimony from Weisheit, lawyers, the children’s parents and first responders who were at an Evansville home in 2010 when the bodies of 8-year-old Alyssa Lynch and 5-year-old Caleb Lynch were recovered in the fire ruins.
Alyssa’s body was in a closet. Caleb’s body was on a mattress, restrained with duct tape. A railroad flare was in his underwear and another was under his body.
“There is no excuse or explanation for what I did,” Weisheit, 50, said on Oct. 16, adding that he wants to live and improve the lives of other people in prison.
The children’s mother, Lisa Lynch, was in a relationship with him when the fire was set 16 years ago while she was at work.

Before the fire, Weisheit had his eye on an engagement ring, but the relationship with Lynch was breaking down. He quit his job, withdrew money from the bank and canceled the ring order, telling the jeweler that he would soon leave the country, said lawyer Tyler Banks of the Indiana attorney general’s office.
“Clemency is meant for those who show genuine remorse and hold true value for human life,” Lynch told the board by video. “Nothing about the murder of my children showed mercy, humanity or remorse.”
Their father, Steven Lynch, said he would accept a life sentence.
An email seeking comment from Weisheit's lawyer, Joseph Perkovich, about the parole board's recommendation was not immediately returned Wednesday.

Perkovich acknowledged the “unspeakable" crimes when he spoke to the board on Oct. 19 but said Weisheit has a history of head injuries and mental health problems that didn't get enough attention at his 2013 trial.
The board said it considered information about Weisheit's mental health but found it “does not greatly distinguish his situation from a vast majority of incarcerated individuals.”

title: Conservative activists O'Keefe, Higby charged with unlawful voting in Minnesota
summary: Conservative activists James O’Keefe and Cam Higby have been charged with unlawful voting and identity theft in Minnesota after a prosecutor said they gave false names to poll workers during the state's primary election
story: Conservative activists James O’Keefe and Cam Higby have been charged with unlawful voting and identity theft in Minnesota after a prosecutor said they gave false names to poll workers during the state's primary election

MINNEAPOLIS -- Conservative activists James O'Keefe and Cam Higby were charged Wednesday with unlawful voting and identity theft after a Minnesota prosecutor said they gave false names to poll workers during the state's primary election. The men recorded the exchanges for a video to expose what they say are vulnerabilities in the state's voting laws.

Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty announced the felony charges at a news conference. She said O'Keefe, 42, of West Palm Beach, Florida, and Higby, 26, of Covington, Washington, wore costumes and used the names of registered state voters while starting the “vouching” process in the Aug. 11 primary. The process provides a way for unregistered voters who lack proof of their current address to register and vote after signing an oath of eligibility.
Poll workers were suspicious and reported their behavior. Moriarty said the situation shows that “the system for identifying misconduct and responding to it functioned well during the primary.”

O'Keefe, who founded and later was ousted as leader of Project Veritas, came to notoriety by publishing undercover sting-style videos like the one made at the Minnesota polling places. He was not immediately available for comment, and court records do not name an attorney to comment on his behalf.
Higby did not immediately respond to an email requesting comment and did not have an attorney in court records. Neither of them has had an opportunity to enter a plea.

Minnesota allows registered voters to “vouch” for another voter in the same precinct by signing an oath attesting to the second person’s identity and that they live in the precinct. The person being vouched for also must sign an oath attesting to their identity and eligibility to vote, and must also provide their Minnesota driver's license or identification card number or the last four digits of their Social Security number.

The process is rarely used but is most commonly done by older adults who have not updated their address on a driver’s license because they no longer drive. In the November 2024 election, fewer than 0.6% of votes cast used the process, according to the Minnesota Secretary of State’s office website.

In their video that was posted to Youtube on Aug. 13, O'Keefe, Higby and others dressed in costumes similar to attire worn by some Muslims and used fake accents while asking about the vouching process at multiple Minneapolis voting sites. Higby's face was covered and when talking to poll workers O'Keefe referred to him as his wife.
Moriarty said both men “identified themselves using names of registered voters in the precinct without those voters' knowledge or permission.”

The poll workers noticed the “strange behavior” and flagged it to election officials, Moriarty said, who asked police to investigate. The men stopped short of signing the oath required for vouching, but Moriarty said that giving false names and starting the process was enough to justify the felony charges.
“Free and fair elections are the bedrock of democracy, and their protection is one of our highest priorities,” Moriarty said.

O'Keefe's organization, O'Keefe Media Group, posted a statement and the video on its website and said the men presented “an intentionally extreme scenario to expose what they see as the lunacy of the state’s 'vouching' system.”

“The team wanted to determine how election workers would respond, what safeguards they would describe, and how far they would allow the vouching process to proceed,” the statement said. “Not every election worker reacted the same way. While several workers explained how the undercover team could proceed under the vouching rules, others became suspicious of the group and took issue with the investigation. Some workers communicated concerns about the team over their radios.”

David Becker, a former Justice Department official and the executive director of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, said he wasn’t aware of any examples of vouching leading to organized or widespread fraud. But he said there have been more efforts recently by those pushing voter fraud claims to commit questionable acts themselves.
“Impersonating another voter is a very serious crime,” Becker said.

Voter identification laws vary from state to state. Thirty-six states have laws requesting or requiring voters to show some form of identification at the polls, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures, but that identification can range from a photo ID to things like a utility bill or bank statement.

In the remaining 14 states and Washington, D.C., voters can cast a ballot without showing ID. They must verify their identity in various other ways, like signing an affidavit or providing personal information like birth date, name or address.

Some states, like Minnesota, allow election officials or other registered voters to vouch for people without a current ID. Alaska and New Hampshire, for instance, allow officials like a clerk or a supervisor to verify a voter’s identity if they know the voter personally. North Dakota allows people who lack identification cards because of a disability to have an attester certify that they are a qualified voter. West Virginia allows an adult who has known a voter for at least six months to sign a sworn statement verifying the voter’s identity.
___ Boone reported from Boise, Idaho. Associated Press writer Ali Swenson contributed.

title: Cornell faculty to begin voting on no-confidence resolution over handling of rape
summary: Cornell University faculty will begin voting Wednesday on a proposed no-confidence resolution in the university’s administration amid frustration over its handling of a woman’s report that she was gang raped at a fraternity house in 2024
story: Cornell University faculty will begin voting Wednesday on a proposed no-confidence resolution in the university’s administration amid frustration over its handling of a woman’s report that she was gang raped at a fraternity house in 2024

Cornell University faculty will meet Wednesday to conclude debate and begin voting on a proposed no-confidence resolution in the university’s administration following widespread frustration over its response to a woman who reported she was gang raped at a campus fraternity house in 2024.
The meeting comes after an Oct. 14 Faculty Senate meeting at which angry faculty members confronted Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff about the university’s handling of the allegations.

The meeting was closed to the media, but in an audio recording obtained by The Associated Press, Kotlikoff acknowledged some missteps, defended his leadership and asked for more time to implement reforms and push for cultural changes in student social life. He urged faculty to have confidence in his leadership, pointing to an independent investigation into the university’s handling of the case that he said could lead to meaningful reforms.

A woman identified in court documents by the pseudonym Jane Doe filed a lawsuit last month alleging that seven Chi Phi fraternity members sexually assaulted or exploited her in October 2024 and that Cornell mishandled her complaints. All seven men have denied her allegations.

The criminal investigation by Cornell’s police department stalled after the local district attorney declined to pursue charges. But in an interview with The New York Times, Kotlikoff said he never followed up to learn what had happened to the woman or the criminal investigation.

Asked by a faculty member whether he read the Cornell Police Department’s report on the rape allegations, Kotlikoff acknowledged that he had not, but said that was because the police investigation was confidential and university policy is that top administrators shouldn’t have a role in criminal investigations.
“I really reject the idea that I had no interest in it or was not concerned about it,” Kotlikoff said.
He insisted experienced leadership was necessary to confront problems. Replacing a president would harm Cornell’s reputation, Kotlikoff said.
Faculty also questioned Cornell’s handling of a disciplined student’s return to campus, including his assignment to a shared dorm room with a roommate unaware of his disciplinary history.

After Kotlikoff departed, a string of faculty speakers said they had lost confidence in the administration’s ability to combat sexual assault on campus. Some Faculty Senate members warned that a hasty no-confidence vote would do little to address the underlying problems.

Wednesday’s meeting is scheduled to begin at 3:30 p.m. and will be closed to the public and media. Electronic voting will open afterward and remain open through Nov. 6. Individual votes will be anonymous.
A no-confidence vote by the faculty would be largely symbolic, but could send a message to the university’s trustees, who ultimately decide who leads it.
Kotlikoff became the university’s interim president in July 2024 and took the job permanently last year.

He’s faced challenges including a dining and custodial workers strike, ire over his decision last year to pay $60 million to settle Trump administration civil rights investigations, and accusations from activists that his administration stifled campus protests.

title: Police arrest three in school shooting plot in Atlanta area
summary: Police in Georgia say three people, including two juveniles, have been arrested in connection with a plot to carry out a shooting at a high school in metro Atlanta
story: Police in Georgia say three people, including two juveniles, have been arrested in connection with a plot to carry out a shooting at a high school in metro Atlanta
Three people, including two juveniles, have been arrested in connection with an alleged plot to carry out a shooting at a high school in metro Atlanta, authorities said Tuesday.
The announcement comes less than two weeks after a 16-year-old boy killed three children and a teacher in a shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in central Oregon.

The FBI discovered threatening posts online from one of the trio and worked with local police to make the arrests on Oct. 20 and 23, apprehending two in Georgia and the third in California, the Canton Police Department said in a news release. They found weapons and ammunition.

They were arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder. Police said one of the suspects is 21 years old and another 17, but they didn't provide the age of the third suspect other than saying he is a juvenile. The third suspect is also accused of disrupting or interfering with the operation of public schools.
Cherokee County School Superintendent Dr. Mary Elizabeth Davis said that the juvenile is a former student at Cherokee High School, WSB-TV reported.
The investigation is active, Canton police said. The department didn't provide details about what exactly they are accused of planning to do or how close they were to doing it.
The Canton Police Department and the Cherokee County School District did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Kelety reported from Phoenix.

title: Inmate's escape is just the latest problem for Tennessee's troubled prison system
summary: The weekend escape of a Tennessee inmate who was convicted of murdering a co-worker was just the latest black eye for the state’s troubled prison system, coming only weeks after the failed execution of Christa Pike
story: The weekend escape of a Tennessee inmate who was convicted of murdering a co-worker was just the latest black eye for the state’s troubled prison system, coming only weeks after the failed execution of Christa Pike

NASHVILLE, Tenn. -- The weekend escape of a Tennessee inmate who was convicted of murdering a co-worker was just the latest black eye for the state's troubled prison system, coming only weeks after the failed execution of Christa Pike.

Jacob Morley was last known to have been in Marion, Illinois, on Tuesday. Authorities say he stole a truck from a nearby farm after escaping late Sunday from the Northwest Correctional Complex near Tiptonville, Tennessee, and abandoned it Tuesday behind a strip mall in Marion, which is about 120 miles (193 kilometers) north of the lockup.
Police have been trying to determine where Morley went after ditching the truck.

Authorities haven't received any credible tips that Morley remained in the Marion area or reports of other vehicles that have gone missing in the city since Tuesday, Marion Police Chief David Fitts said Wednesday.
Morley's escape is the latest blemish for Tennessee's prison system.
After the failed execution of Pike last month, Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada announced his resignation after less than three years on the job.
State Sen. Tom Hatcher said the resignation couldn't come soon enough.

“We need new leadership,” the Republican from Blount County said. “We're doing oversight work behind the scenes about several of our prisons. We're just waiting to see who our next governor will be and who is the next commissioner.”

Understaffing is a big problem at Tennessee's prisons, said Hatcher, who is the chairman of a legislative subcommittee looking into the prison system. He noted that Strada didn't show up for the last oversight meeting, which happened days before Pike's execution date.

During a subcommittee hearing, prison officials said they had 470 open jobs among their 6,000-person workforce. They also warned that a 2022 law requiring inmates to serve more of their sentences was increasing prison populations and could lead to overcrowding.
Prison leadership also isn't transparent about problems and doesn't accept oversight well, even though the problems repeat themselves, Hatcher said.
“Until we get someone who wants to look at all of this, we're going to keep having problems,” he said.
A prison spokesperson said the agency was not commenting at this time.
The prison Morley escaped from has had several violent attacks between inmates and by employees in recent years.
District Attorney Danny H. Goodman Jr. is overseeing the prosecution of 19 cases stemming from indictments this summer at the Northwest Correctional Complex.
The cases include five inmates killed behind bars and assaults against staff and inmates. Former prison employees charged with aggravated assault are among the people named in 50 indictments.
Goodman said there is no evidence that Morley was involved in any of those attacks.

Staffing at the isolated prison, which is about 90 miles (145 kilometers) from Memphis, Tennessee, has been a major problem, Goodman said, noting that although he suspects that understaffing could have contributed to the escape or the violence, he doesn't have any proof.
“There is a huge shortage of staff there,” Goodman said. “The ones that are there, they have to work so much. It’s not unusual for them to have to work double shifts.”
There's no evidence yet that anyone helped Morley escape, but the investigation is ongoing, Goodman said.

Authorities said Morley, 28, slipped through a fence in his prison clothes late Sunday night before walking to the nearby farm and stealing the truck. He is white, 5 feet 11 inches (1.8 meters) tall and weighs 240 pounds (109 kilograms). He has brown hair and green eyes.

Morley is serving a life sentence for killing co-worker Cody Birchfield in 2022. Birchfield’s body was found in a box under Morley’s home after he had been missing for a few weeks. The two lived in Carter County, in eastern Tennessee.
Collins reported from Columbia, South Carolina.

title: How Trump's immigration crackdown sparked a backlash that could boomerang
summary: Donald Trump roared back into office two years ago partly on the power of immigration
story: Donald Trump roared back into office two years ago partly on the power of immigration

MINNEAPOLIS -- When Donald Trump was running for president two years ago, Americans’ television screens were filled with images of migrant chaos. There were tent camps on both sides of the border, caravans of people trudging through Central America and concerns about newcomers overwhelming social services.

That turmoil faded as President Joe Biden tightened immigration enforcement after Trump clamped down even more. Now any chaos is on American streets, where violent and even deadly clashes have defined a deportation campaign that's designed to fulfill hardliners' goals of uprooting anyone in the country illegally.

The shift helps explain why Trump's effort to fulfill his promises has turned into a backlash, undermining one of the core issues that fueled his return to the White House. While Trump maintains some support for his handling of the border, polling shows voters disapprove of his approach to immigration, a striking turnaround that could undermine Republican attempts to maintain control of Congress in the midterms.

“The American people supported strong border security,” said Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat who has become a prominent critic of the administration’s policies. “What they got instead was shredding the Constitution, mass deportations and killing American citizens on the streets of Minneapolis.”
Trump's allies say the president is the victim of his own success.

“The disaster at the border and the impunity of people just walking over and being released into the country was hard to ignore,” said Mark Krikorian, executive director of the Center for Immigration Studies. Trump dramatically reduced illegal border crossings, Krikorian said, “and that’s often politically bad."

Krikorian praised Trump for adopting low profile but highly effective sweeps that have achieved month after month of record arrests. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers arrested almost 51,000 immigrants in the country illegally in August, according to the Department of Homeland Security, up from 49,000 in July and 43,000 in June. An estimated 660,000 people have been deported in the past fiscal year, according to the Migration Policy Institute, short of the administration’s goal of 1 million annually.
Biden's immigration policies remain a regular target for Republicans this year. Trump said at a recent Florida rally that Democrats let migrants “pour across our borders from all over the world.”
“If they win in the midterms, they'll do it again,” he warned.

In 2024, Trump  warned repeatedly of an immigrant “invasion.” “They’re poisoning the blood of our country,” he said of people crossing the border illegally. He insisted, falsely, that immigrants were behind spikes in crime and eating household pets.

Even as Trump drew criticism for his rhetoric, his focus on the issue resonated with voters who had seen illegal immigration soar during the Biden administration, with border arrests from Mexico reaching a record 250,000 in December 2023.

Trump's victory seemed poised to reshape immigration politics. Forty-six Democrats in the House and a dozen in the Senate joined Republicans in voting for the Laken Riley Act, a bill named after a Georgia student killed by a man in the country illegally. The law requires detention without bond for noncitizens accused of murder and other violent crimes.

After Trump took office, he cranked deportations into higher gear. Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Maryland resident, was one of the people caught up in that net. Despite a court order forbidding it, the administration sent him to his native El Salvador, where he was confined to that country's notorious central prison that was also used to house other Trump deportees.

The U.S. Supreme Court directed the administration to “facilitate” Abrego Garcia's return, and Van Hollen flew to El Salvador to meet with him. Some Democrats questioned the wisdom of confronting Trump on an issue where the president was so popular, the senator recalled. Now his party is more emboldened on the issue.
“We’ve gone from some of that sniping on the sidelines to a clear vote among Democrats to defund ICE,” Van Hollen said.

The early face of the Trump crackdown was top Border Patrol commander Gregory Bovino, who swaggered through raids in tactical gear and deployed forces to Los Angeles and Chicago, where he led a helicopter raid on an apartment building.

But Minneapolis was the turning point. More than 2,000 federal officers were sent to the city, and scenes of masked agents spilling from convoys of unmarked vehicles became commonplace. Tens of thousands of protesters took to the streets.

Two U.S. citizens — Renee Good and Alex Pretti, both 37 — were killed during confrontations with agents. In the weeks that followed, the White House pushed aside Bovino and Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem.

Michael Pretti, Alex's father, said this week that the family is still troubled by the bystander videos of the shooting. He had a holstered gun that he was legally allowed to carry, and none of the footage shows him brandishing the weapon or attacking federal agents in the moments before he was killed.
“I think it haunts many Americans to see a U.S. citizen who was peaceful and in his community shot multiple times on the back, in the back, while on the ground,” he told reporters.
Arrests dropped after the killings, although they eventually returned to record numbers. But the politics became more complicated, and Republicans’ immigration message has fractured.

There are hardliners like U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee, who is vowing more deportations as she runs for governor. And there's Cuban-American Florida Rep. Maria-Elena Salazar, who criticized Trump’s migrant crackdown in a campaign advertisement filmed outside the White House.

Salazar has sponsored legislation that would allow immigrants who are in the country illegally to remain as long as they have otherwise followed the law. Among the sponsors is Republican Rep. Gabe Evans, the grandson of a Mexican immigrant, who is trying to distinguish himself from Trump while running in a Colorado swing district.
In New Hampshire, former Sen. John Sununu, running for an open Senate seat, has been critical of ICE tactics and the agency's use of masks to conceal agents' identities.

Republicans often try to connect immigration to voters' concerns about high prices. Ohio Sen. Jon Husted blasts Democratic opponent Sherrod Brown as someone who “voted to raise your taxes repeatedly and give those tax dollars to illegals.”

“Republicans are trying to turn voters against Democrats because of what Joe Biden did in failing to control the border effectively,” said Frank Sharry, a longtime immigrants' rights activist who consults with the centrist Democratic group Third Way. “So they’re trying to define Democrats as being for open borders and not serious about removing criminals.”
But that comes as many Democratic candidates are shifting away from Biden-era messaging about immigration.
In Texas, Senate candidate James Talarico calls himself a “border security Democrat” who wants to hire more Border Patrol officers and increase the use of surveillance technology.
Talarico criticizes many of Trump’s immigration policies as wasteful, but doesn’t hold back when it comes to criticizing the last Democratic president.
“Joe Biden and his administration failed us on our southern border,” he said in a July press conference in a Texas county on the Mexico border.
Even some of the most liberal Democratic candidates, like Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed, are careful to note that they want strong borders.
“I don’t know of a candidate who’s in a swing race who’s saying anything other than ‘We’ve got to secure the border’ and ‘We’ve got to remove criminals,’” Sharry said.
Riccardi reported from Denver. Associated Press writer Aaron Kessler in Washington contributed to this report.

title: United flight turned around after passenger allegedly said he'd 'hijack' plane
summary: An airplane passenger was arrested for allegedly writing that he was going to “hijack” the plane, forcing the United flight to be diverted back to Las Vegas shortly after takeoff
story: An airplane passenger was arrested for allegedly writing that he was going to “hijack” the plane, forcing the United flight to be diverted back to Las Vegas shortly after takeoff

LAS VEGAS -- An airplane passenger was arrested for allegedly writing a message while midair that he was going to “hijack” the plane, forcing the United flight to be diverted back to Las Vegas shortly after takeoff Saturday.

The 25-year-old allegedly communicated that he was “gonna hijack this” plane — although he used an expletive — and “crash ur row only,” according to a copy of the criminal complaint. The document doesn't specify exactly how the message was sent or to whom it was directed.

Las Vegas police said they detained the man after a report of a person making “terroristic threats” on the Saturday night flight that had been headed to Newark, New Jersey. He was arrested on charges of making a threat or providing false information regarding an act of terrorism, which carries a possible sentence of 1 to 20 years in prison.
An attorney listed for the man did not immediately return a request for comment. His initial court appearance is scheduled for Tuesday.
The scheduled redeye flight returned to the airport less than an hour after departing, according to Flightradar24 data.

United confirmed that the flight with 150 passengers on board returned safely to Las Vegas to address a “potential security concern.” The flight was delayed overnight and departed for Newark on Sunday morning.
The Federal Aviation Administration confirmed it will investigate the incident and said in an email to The Associated Press there have been over 1,400 unruly passenger incidents so far in 2026.
Associated Press writer Rio Yamat contributed to this report.

title: Hunter Biden laptop issue resurfaces as judge scolds prosecutors over case against ex-FBI officials
summary: A federal judge has scolded the Justice Department for its unorthodox handling of a criminal case against two former FBI officials accused of making false statements to Congress about their participation in and knowledge of investigations involving Hun...
story: A federal judge has scolded the Justice Department for its unorthodox handling of a criminal case against two former FBI officials accused of making false statements to Congress about their participation in and knowledge of investigations involving Hun...

WASHINGTON -- A federal judge on Tuesday scolded prosecutors for their unorthodox handling of a criminal case against two former FBI officials accused of making false statements to Congress about their knowledge of a laptop the Justice Department says belonged to Hunter Biden, the son of former President Joe Biden.

U.S. Magistrate Zia Faruqui rejected an amended criminal complaint filed overnight by the Justice Department that added a new obstruction charge against the two former officials, Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, after concluding that it was improperly submitted. Such charging documents require sign-off from a judge that probable cause exists to believe a crime was committed by a defendant, but this complaint was filed straight to the docket with no court approval.

The ruling came during a dramatic, hourslong hearing in which an agent who worked the case conceded under defense lawyer questioning that the investigation was launched after a July speech from President Donald Trump on election interference and that the inquiry was mandated by FBI Director Kash Patel. The agent, Bryan Witt, suggested he had been begrudgingly assigned to the investigation and had regarded it as a “huge distraction” from other casework.
“I had concerns that this would be political,” he said.

The testimony was elicited by defense lawyers looking to bolster their argument that the prosecution was politically motivated. Faruqui's rebuke, meanwhile, marked a setback for a Justice Department that has employed unusual maneuvers in splashy investigative actions ahead of next week’s midterm elections. Newly unsealed documents in a separate case, for instance, revealed that prosecutors are attempting to again prosecute former FBI Director James Comey, an outspoken Trump critic, in a manner that Comey's lawyers say is legally invalid.

The judge said he had never before seen a prosecutor file an unsigned criminal complaint, describing it as “inappropriate” given defendants’ presumption of innocence. He ticked off several atypical aspects of the case, including the decision to file charges via criminal complaint, which the judge noted is more often used when the government has disrupted an active crime or needs to take a defendant into custody immediately because of a potential danger to society.
“Everything is a little sideshow on top of a sideshow,” Faruqui said, saying prosecutors appeared to be throwing “gas” on defendants’ assertions that there is nothing typical about this case.

Witt testified that Patel had directed that the investigation be opened after a Trump primetime address in July in which the president amplified debunked theories about the 2020 election he lost and elevated his yearslong push to raise doubts about the legitimacy of U.S. elections.

Among the grievances the White House raised at the time was a disputed FBI intelligence report about an alleged effort by China to influence the election through fraudulent driver's licenses. Trump and some allies have cited the memo as proof of what they contend was a Chinese plot to intervene in favor of Joe Biden, his Democratic opponent. But senior FBI officials ordered the document recalled because of concerns about the validity of the intelligence.

Witt, who works in Kansas City, Missouri, said Patel assigned the investigation to his office and said he was directed to investigate Floris and other officials who were believed to be involved in recalling the memo.

He said the basis for the investigation was Trump administration suspicions that the FBI in 2020 had suppressed intelligence that could have been harmful to the Bidens. He said he understood the fact that the inquiry was opened in the aftermath of a Trump speech, and at the behest of the FBI director, made it appear like a “political" investigation. Patel and FBI leadership, he said, maintained a keen interest in the probe.
“They wanted us to investigate aggressively,” Witt said.

Even before that testimony was given, Mary Dohrmann, another lawyer for Floris, broached what she called the “elephant in the room,” saying “evidence is mounting that this prosecution is about some political football — and not the law or the facts.”
The case, announced Friday, accuses Floris and Benavides of falsely playing down their knowledge about a laptop the Justice Department says Hunter Biden abandoned at a computer repair shop in 2019.

Prosecutors say they claimed to have no independent insight into the FBI's possession of the laptop while being interviewed in 2023 in a separate congressional investigation related to the Biden family. In reality, according to the criminal complaint, the two participated in numerous discussions about the laptop in their capacity as leaders of the since-disbanded FBI Foreign Influence Task Force that was set up to monitor foreign influence.
The Justice Department contends that the defendants' professed lack of knowledge allowed them to avoid further questioning about Hunter Biden and impeded the congressional investigation.

But Ron Safer, a lawyer for Benavides, challenged that assertion during the hearing Tuesday. He suggested that his client had no motive to lie and pointed out that Benavides was questioned in 2023, long after he had left his position on the task force, about events that had occurred several years earlier.

“What evidence have you uncovered that in September of 2023, Mr. Benavides remembered the correct answers, in your view, to the questions asked about Hunter Biden but gave knowingly incorrect answers?” Safer asked Witt.

The prosecution revisits a tangled saga that roiled the final weeks of the 2020 race after the New York Post revealed the existence of a laptop it said had been dropped off by the younger Biden at a Delaware computer repair shop about a year earlier.

The Post said it had obtained a hard drive of the laptop from Rudy Giuliani, a close ally of President Donald Trump, and reported on some of the contents of the computer, including emails that appeared to show some of Hunter Biden's foreign business dealings.

The curious circumstances of the laptop’s discovery raised concerns among Democrats and former intelligence officials about the possibility of Russian involvement, particularly when the Trump administration’s own intelligence community had assessed that Moscow was attempting to undermine the candidacy of Democratic nominee Joe Biden, who went on to defeat Trump in 2020, and as Giuliani had traveled abroad looking for dirt on the Bidens.

But Trump's then-national intelligence director, John Ratcliffe, quickly sought to quell speculation about the laptop's provenance by saying there were no signs it had anything to do with Russian actors.
The younger Biden was ultimately convicted on gun and tax charges. President Joe Biden pardoned his son in late 2024.

title: 'Picasso of Pumpkin Carvers' brings artistry to a Halloween tradition
summary: Carving pumpkins is a Halloween tradition
story: Carving pumpkins is a Halloween tradition

HALF MOON BAY, Calif. -- When fall arrives and leaves start changing color, Mike Valladao, a systems engineer at a cybersecurity company, slips into his alter ego, “Farmer Mike,” also known as the “Picasso of Pumpkin Carvers.”

Farmer Mike has been chiseling whimsical faces and comical creatures into big pumpkins for more than four decades. Wearing his trademark orange overalls and farmer hat, he's sculpted hundreds of gourds into ghoulish faces, seaside landscapes, witches, dragons and pop culture figures such as Yoda and Charlie Brown.
Valladao doesn’t have any formal artistic training, but he's always looking for inspiration. He gets ideas from looking at art in a museum or just walking down the street.
“Sometimes I’ll look at somebody and I’ll think, oh, I like the teeth or I like ears or the way the nostrils flare,” Valladao said.

This year, “Farmer Mike” celebrated 40 years of Halloween artistry at the Half Moon Bay Art & Pumpkin Festival, which is held in mid-October and is best known for its giant pumpkin weigh-off. At the two-day festival on the coast south of San Francisco, Valladao works on stage so people can watch.

Valladao stumbled into his artistic hobby after he began growing big pumpkins at his San Jose home in the mid-1980s. He didn’t know what to do with the massive gourds, so he pulled out a knife and started slicing faces into them.
“I’m an engineer by trade and I tend to look at it as building something the same way I would build a piece of hardware, one layer at a time,” he said.

In 1986, festival organizers saw a picture of Valladao’s pumpkins and invited him to showcase his carving skills in Half Moon Bay, where his family opened the town’s first feed and seed store in the 19th century. He grew an 800-pound (363-kilogram) pumpkin once, but it was a lot of work, so he doesn’t participate in the giant pumpkin contest.

His art has since taken him to different parts of the country, including an appearance on “The Tonight Show.” He has gotten requests to carve pumpkins at venues such as the San Diego Zoo, the California Academy of Sciences and the State Fair of Texas.
He uses Atlantic pumpkins that weigh from 100 to 1,000 pounds (45 to 454 kilograms). They have thick skins that allow him to cut protruding facial features shallow or deep.

“It’s really about the illusion of depth,” Valladao said. “I can make it so that it’s three-dimensional, such that the eyes are inset and the nose sticks out. So it’s a little bit of carving, but it’s just adding a little more magic to it.”
Valladao said he doesn’t name his creations because he recognizes the ephemeral nature of his art, which only lasts a few days.
“It never really bothers me when a pumpkin starts to age because in some cases they’ll build character,” Valladao said.
And there are always more pumpkins to be carved.
After 40 years at Half Moon Bay, Valladao doesn’t have any plans to hang up his carving knives.
“It’s fun, it’s enjoyable and, quite frankly, it’s a piece of me,” he said.

title: Special master could evaluate Justice Department's claims of noncitizens on California voter rolls
summary: A federal judge says he is considering appointing a special master to evaluate claims by the Trump administration that California has some 20,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls
story: A federal judge says he is considering appointing a special master to evaluate claims by the Trump administration that California has some 20,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls

Los Angeles -- A federal judge on Tuesday said he was considering appointing a special master to evaluate claims by the Trump administration that California has some 20,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls and to determine whether counties would be able to separate any ballots belonging to ineligible voters.

U.S. District Judge David O. Carter was overseeing a hearing in a lawsuit filed by the Justice Department, which is seeking to prevent California from counting ballots from thousands of people it alleges are noncitizens.

Carter said it would be too rushed to make a decision without an independent special master who could evaluate the substance of both sides’ claims. He said that could be completed before the state’s Dec. 11 deadline to certify the election results.

It is not clear what would happen if a special master did find a substantial number of noncitizen voters on the federal government's list or whether it would affect the certification of California's election results. The 20,000 people on the DOJ's list constitute only a small fraction of California's 23 million voters.

Voting has been well underway for weeks in California in the midterm election that concludes next Tuesday. Alleged voting by noncitizens has been a key focus of President Donald Trump's administration with control of Congress at stake, though available data indicates occurrences are exceedingly rare.

The Republican administration sued election officials in California in mid-October, accusing them of failing to meet a 48-hour deadline to review its list of 20,000 people it alleged were likely noncitizens on the state’s voter rolls.

The Justice Department made a similar request in Washington state this week for the state to sequester ballots submitted by hundreds of people it suspects are not U.S. citizens. Meanwhile, another lawsuit filed in Alaska last week seeks to delay certification of the vote if the Republican incumbent running for U.S. Senate doesn’t win. All three states have House or Senate races that will help determine the balance of power in the nation's Capitol.
Although Carter said he was open to appointing a special master, he said he will not issue an official order until Wednesday.

The judge said he wanted to vet the federal government’s list. He emphasized his concerns that siding with the federal government at this stage could mean illegally making substantial changes to election procedure while voting is underway.

But he said the special master also could investigate California’s claims that it could not logistically separate the ballots in time for the election certification deadline in December, an assertion the federal government has contested.

Carter rarely spoke throughout the hearing, but he did express skepticism about why the federal government was suing California rather than seeking to address alleged noncitizen voting through criminal prosecutions. He referenced the federal government's recent arrest in October of 28 people across California accused of illegally registering to vote.
“You got a remedy for goodness sakes — go out and indict,” Carter said from the bench.
Prosecutors with the federal government argued that the U.S. had an interest in preventing noncitizens from voting in the first place.
"We want to stop the illegal voting,” First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said. “We don’t want to chase it later.”
Carter also seemed to respond to warnings that local county clerks who don't heed the federal government's demands could be criminally prosecuted.
"This court believes it would be wise that any threats to state and county election employees cease immediately,” Carter said before abruptly leaving the courtroom.
Essayli argued Tuesday that the Justice Department’s demands would not significantly disrupt the ongoing election.
“We have not asked to void any ballots,” he said. Instead, the government was seeking to work with California officials to “safeguard” the election.
He said testimony would explain how the government's list of 20,000 names was compiled.
“The case rises and falls on the credibility” of the flagged names, he told the judge, arguing the state has an obligation to investigate before counting those voters' ballots.

California officials previously argued that once a completed mail ballot is returned, it is separated from the envelope that contains voters' identification. That would make it impossible to separate ballots that have already been submitted, the state said. More than 3 million ballots have already been returned.

Lawyers for California and Los Angeles County said the federal government has not specified how or when it obtained the voter file, leaving open the possibility the list was inaccurate or outdated. They specifically questioned the government’s reliance on a private, third-party service to determine Social Security numbers used in their effort.

M. Patrick Moore, a lawyer for the Los Angeles County registrar's office, also argued that the county would cooperate if the federal government wanted to criminally prosecute noncitizens who illegally voted.
“If an individual who is a noncitizen votes, there will be record of that, and the county will provide that record” to the federal courts, Moore said in court Tuesday.
He added that if the federal government believes the election was compromised, there are legal processes for contesting the outcome.
Tuesday's hearing largely revolved around the reliability of the federal government's list. Los Angeles County officials found that a small sample of people on it were indeed citizens.

The federal agent who conducted the investigation — which required roughly 800 federal employees who manually checked each name — said in an affidavit that the county's findings were false. The filing did concede that some names of citizens could have been mistakenly included.

title: Hayden Panettiere's death ruled accidental by South Carolina police
summary: A South Carolina coroner previously confirmed Panettiere died from an accidental drug overdose that included fentanyl.
story: The death of Hayden Panettiere has been ruled accidental, South Caroline police announced Wednesday.

Greenville Police Department said the investigation into Panettiere's death has been concluded "based on the Medical Examiner's determination and the findings of the investigation," and the actor's death was officially ruled accidental.
Last month, a South Carolina coroner confirmed Panettiere died from an accidental drug overdose that included fentanyl. There were no signs of trauma, the coroner's office said.

Emergency responders were called to a residence where Panettiere, 36, had been staying in Greenville, South Carolina, on the afternoon of Aug. 16. Despite "advanced cardiac life support measures," she was pronounced dead there, the Greenville County Coroner's Office said.'

Panettiere's on-again, off-again boyfriend Brian Hickerson and his brother Zach were at the scene of her death, according to a police report obtained by CBS News. The Hickersons made the 911 call that brought first responders to the apartment.

Authorities, including the Drug Enforcement Administration, were investigating the circumstances of Panettiere's death. Police previously said that a preliminary investigation "has not indicated any signs of foul play or suspicious circumstances."

title: Jay-Z to headline 2027 Super Bowl halftime show
summary: The NFL, Apple Music and Roc Nation announced Monday night that Jay-Z will be the featured performer for the halftime festivities on Feb. 14 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.
story: The man who has helped produce the Super Bowl halftime show is stepping into the spotlight: Jay-Z will headline the show himself.
The NFL, Apple Music and Roc Nation announced Monday night that Jay-Z will be the featured performer for the halftime festivities on Feb. 14 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.
The announcement included a short video of Jay-Z sitting in SoFi Stadium surrounded by goats with the caption "GOAT's out of the bag."

After days of speculation, Jay-Z is set to return to the stadium where he closed his "Jay-Z 30" concerts over the weekend. The run began with three shows at Yankee Stadium in New York, continued in London and ended in Southern California.

Jay-Z's Roc Nation has partnered with the NFL since 2019 to advise on and help produce the league's entertainment presentations, including the Super Bowl halftime show. At the time, Jay-Z said he had told NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell, "If this is about me performing at the Super Bowl, then we can just end this conversation now."
Seven years later, Jay-Z is ready to perform after all.
Since then, the headlining halftime show performers have included Shakira and Jennifer Lopez, Rihanna, Kendrick Lamar and The Weeknd, among others.

Jay-Z, born Shawn Carter, has won 25 Grammy Awards and received 89 nominations, the second-most in history behind his wife, Beyoncé — who has performed at two Super Bowls. His catalog includes the albums "Reasonable Doubt," "The Blueprint" and "The Black Album," and hit songs such as "Hard Knock Life (Ghetto Anthem)," "99 Problems" and "Empire State of Mind," his collaboration with Alicia Keys.
His 1996 debut, "Reasonable Doubt," was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame last year.

Jay-Z's career has extended into music publishing, artist management and sports. He co-founded Roc-A-Fella Records and founded Roc Nation in 2008, building it into an entertainment company that works with artists and athletes.
Jay-Z became the first rapper inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2017 and joined the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2021.
Bad Bunny performed at last season's Super Bowl in February. His songs had sharp gains across streaming charts, playlists and music discovery platforms in the hours following the show.

The next morning, the Puerto Rican superstar held the top six spots on Spotify's Top 50 U.S. chart, with another song coming in at No. 8. Eleven other Bad Bunny songs were ranking in Spotify's Top 50 U.S. chart at the time.

title: Eric Bauza, actor who voiced Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, dies at 46
summary: Eric Bauza, the Emmy-winning actor who voiced iconic "Looney Tunes" characters Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, died on Sunday, according to his manager. He was 46.
story: Eric Bauza, the Emmy-winning actor who voiced iconic "Looney Tunes" characters Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, died on Sunday, according to his manager. He was 46.

"Eric was a unique and versatile voice actor who was loved by everyone he knew and worked with," said Judy Coppage, Bauza's manager. "His sudden passing is a shock to all of us, and he will be deeply missed. It's a profound loss for his family, the animation industry and his fans."
Bauza, who was born in Canada, died from hypertensive cardiovascular disease, according to the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner.
His family posted a brief statement on his Instagram page, adding that more details would come later.

Bauza had more than 400 acting credits listed on his IMDb page. In addition to voicing Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, Bauza is credited with voicing other "Looney Tunes" characters such as Porky Pig, Pepé Le Pew, Marvin the Martian, Elmer Fudd, Foghorn Leghorn, Tweety Bird and Road Runner. He also voiced characters in the most recent "Space Jam" film, alongside LeBron James.

Beyond "Looney Tunes," Bauza was known for his voice work on shows such as "Avatar: The Last Airbender," "Puss in Boots," "Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles," "Woody Woodpecker," "Bob's Burgers" and "Teen Titans Go!"
A statement from Warner Bros. Chairman Channing Dungey and Warner Bros. Pictures Animation President and CCO Bill Damaschke noted Bauza's impact on the "Looney Tunes" franchise.

"Eric Bauza was a unique voice talent who brought joy and laughter to millions around the world. During his 15 years at Warner Bros. Animation, he was the voice of Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck among countless other characters. He followed in the footsteps of giants like Mel Blanc," the statement said. "Eric said that carrying on the legendary legacy of the Looney Tunes was among the greatest honors of his life. In addition to his incredible talent, Eric was a treasured part of our animation family. Our hearts go out to his loved ones."
Bauza won Children's and Family Emmy Awards in 2022, 2023 and 2025 and was nominated in 2026. He was also nominated for five Daytime Emmy Awards from 2016 to 2021.
He joined CBS LA in August to discuss his latest film and the newest "Looney Tunes" installment, "Coyote vs. Acme."

"All of my work is based off of the original voiceover artist, the great Mel Blanc; he was the original. I like to call him the blueprint of these characters," Bauza said. "They're not just voices; these are personalities that we've been familiar with now for 90 years — it's like your oldest family members. So, that's my history with them."
Bauza said his favorite character to voice was Bugs Bunny, but as he got older, he felt more like Daffy Duck.

title: Walter Koenig, actor who played Chekov on "Star Trek," dies at 90
summary: Walter Koenig played Pavel Chekov in the original "Star Trek" television series and several movies.
story: Walter Koenig, the actor who played Pavel Chekov in the original "Star Trek" television series and several movies, has died, his rep confirmed to CBS News. He was 90.
Koenig died Sunday night at his home in the North Hollywood neighborhood of Los Angeles, talent rep Zachery McGinnis said in a statement. He died surrounded by his daughter and niece, McGinnis said.

In "Star Trek," Ensign Chekov was the sole member of the spaceship Enterprise bridge staff from what was the Communist bloc. His friendly, supportive presence showed how the rival nations (in the far-off future in which the show was set) were capable of working together.
Speaking heavily Russian-accented English, Chekov embodied stereotypical Russian personality traits, including fierce pride, love of poetry and blind loyalty.
"Star Trek" ran on NBC from 1966 to 1969 and has had an almost unprecedented afterlife as fans, or Trekkies, kept interest in the show alive.

Koenig was born Sept. 14, 1936, in Chicago, the son of a businessman. He graduated from the University of California, Los Angeles, in 1958, then studied acting at New York's The Neighborhood Playhouse for two years. He began getting television roles in the early 1960s, appearing on "Mr. Novak" and "Ben Casey."
"My heart is heavy," Koenig's castmate, George Takei, said on social media. "Walter was more than Chekov. He was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man, and a loyal friend."
Koenig was the best man at Takei's 2008 wedding to Brad Altman, his partner of more than two decades.
McGinnis noted that Koenig's legacy extended far beyond the screen.

"Through countless convention appearances and interactions with fans, he shared his kindness, wit, and appreciation with everyone fortunate enough to meet him. He understood what Star Trek meant to people and embraced the community that grew around it," McGinnis said. "Thank you, Walter, for the memories, the inspiration, and for boldly going where few have gone before."

Koenig played Chekov in seven "Star Trek" movies starting in 1979, as well as innumerable other spinoffs, including writing a "Star Trek" book, "Chekov's Enterprise," in 1980. The TV show has also inspired two spinoff TV series with new casts, and conventions that draw thousands of fans.
After "Star Trek" ended, Koenig continued acting and wrote scripts for "Family," "The Incredible Hulk" and other shows. He also taught part time at UCLA and other schools.
Koenig also worked in the burgeoning field of computer games, including some with a "Star Trek" theme. In 1995, he took a role in the CD-ROM game "Maximum Surge."

"I'm at a point where I could opt in my life for complacency and a bit of predictability, or I could have one last holler — one last try for adventure," Koenig told The Associated Press in 1995. "I'm of the opinion that adventure is still a very enticing and exciting option."
He returned to the science fiction genre with occasional appearances on the syndicated 1990s TV series "Babylon 5."

title: Notable Deaths in 2026
summary: A look back at the esteemed personalities who've left us this year, who'd touched us with their innovation, creativity and humanity.
story: A look back at the esteemed personalities who left us this year, who touched us with their innovation, creativity and humanity.
By CBSNews.com senior producer David Morgan. The Associated Press contributed to this gallery.

Actor Walter Koenig (Sept. 14, 1936-Oct. 25, 2026) originated the character of Ensign Pavel Chekov, the Starship Enterprise's Russian navigator, during the second season of the TV series "Star Trek." After the original series ended in 1969, he continued playing the character, promoted to lieutenant, in seven theatrical features (concluding with 1994's "Star Trek: Generations"), and, as an admiral, in fan productions (including "Star Trek: New Voyages" and "Star Trek: Renegades").

Born of Russian Jewish immigrant parents, Koenig had several TV credits in the 1960s (including "Ben Casey," "The Alfred Hitchcock Hour," "Gidget," and Gene Roddenberry's "The Lieutenant") before auditioning to play Chekov in 1967. In a 2013 interview with the Television Academy Foundation, Koenig (who said he hadn't watched the first season of "Star Trek") said he was asked to read a very serious scene: "The ship is about to blow up," he said. "This is jeopardy, this is personal risk involved here, and I had to show some sense of command and that I was capable of being an officer at this moment. So, I read it with all of that in mind — the brows furled, the jaws clenched, the teeth tight, and the nostrils flared. And when I got done … they all kind of looked at their feet and said, 'Yeah, well, that's nice, Walt, but can you make it funny?'"

Chekhov would prove to be a lighter-hearted member of the Enterprise crew, speaking with a heavy Russian accent that underscored how 1960s political tensions didn't exist in the 23rd century. The insertion of the youthful Chekov was, Koenig said, inspired by the popularity of The Monkees. "They were looking for an actor or a personality that would appeal to the same demographic that Davy Jones did — kids 8 to 14 years old," he said. "And indeed, my mail was from people who are 8 to 14 years old: 'I think you're groovy,' 'I love your hair' (which was a wig by the way)." Koenig said he never got any hostile mail over the fact that he was a Russian on the Enterprise: "Because these were all kids; they didn't really know too much about the Cold War."

In 2005 Koenig described to the BBC the importance of the multi-cultural (and alien) crew of the Enterprise as they went boldly where no one had gone before: "We were stating tacitly that peoples of all races and creeds, nationalities, could not only co-exist but care for each other deeply, and in doing so we were heralding a future that was very optimistic, and one that I think appealed to the audience," he said. "We would like to believe that the future is not an Armageddon kind of situation, as has been so frequently depicted in film, but one where there's considerably harmony and a kind of one-world environment."

Koenig also wrote several "Star Trek"-themed books and an episode of the "Star Trek" animated series; the comic book series "Raver"; the graphic novel "Things to Come"; and scripts for TV series including "Land of the Lost," "Family" and "The Powers of Matthew Star." Other science fiction appearances were in "Moontrap" and "Babylon 5."

title: How punk rock and MTV inspired opera composer Missy Mazzoli
summary: "Lincoln in the Bardo," based on George Saunders' novel, is the first opera composed by a woman to premiere at the Metropolitan Opera. Missy Mazzoli talks about its creation, and the influence that punk rock and music videos had on her work.
story: On a recent Sunday night in Brooklyn, at a concert by the punk rock band Mannequin Pussy, we found the perhaps unlikely new face of the rarefied world of opera: 45-year-old classical composer Missy Mazzoli.

Asked what she loves about punk music, Mazzoli replied, "I love that it's extreme, that it wears its thoughts and emotions and politics on its sleeve, and that it is just this raw expression of human emotion."
Which sounds exactly like opera!

Mazzoli is taking on one of the biggest stages in the world, the Metropolitan Opera in New York, which is debuting her latest work, "Lincoln in the Bardo." With it, she becomes the first woman to have an opera premiered by the Met in its 143-year history.

Mazzoli's parents bought a piano at a flea market when she was seven. A few years later, she was writing her own music. But it wasn't just classical; she also played in punk bands – and inspiration came from everywhere. "MTV was there for me, when no one else was," she laughed. "And I would watch MTV for hours and hours every day. And so, I can look back to that and say like, 'Oh, my interest in opera makes a lot of sense, because I was watching Guns N' Roses or Sonic Youth, these videos that let you enter a whole different world.'"

"Lincon in the Bardo" is based on the novel by George Saunders, and tells the story of President Lincoln at a pivotal moment. "His 11-year-old son, Willie, died very unexpectedly," Mazzoli said, "and Lincoln was just consumed with grief, and would actually go to the graveyard and visit with his son's body in the days and weeks after his death."
I have no power here.And now I must accept it.My boy is gone!My boy is gone!Peaceful, resplendent, in a new form of being.Willie is dead.My dear little chap, good-bye. – From "Lincoln in the Bardo"

Mazzoli says the opera asks big questions that speak to our time, too. "This is a story that takes place at the height of the Civil War when America is at its most divided," she said. "And the idea of making a work set in a very divided America felt extremely relevant."

To prepare, Mazzoli spent time in actual cemeteries herself.  "For me, opera is the way to explore things that are difficult to talk about," she said. "Think about life and death. We can sing songs about it. But I think that we can sort of get at what the questions are. So, when someone is singing their heart out about love or betrayal or grief, I think words don't do those emotions justice, but singing and music really can."
True to form, "Lincoln in the Bardo" is an enormous production, with elaborate costumes, puppetry, special effects, and even a very large horse who makes a brief appearance at the end of the show.

Royce Vavrek has written the lyrics to Mazzoli's music in six operas. "We really bond because of our shared love of storytelling and theater," he said, "and so I am in charge of sort of the word drama and she is in charge of the musical drama, and together I think we just combust into something way bigger than the sum of our two parts."

Just this summer, they premiered another new work, "The Galloping Cure," which looks at the opioid epidemic. It's a personal topic for both. "I have two cousins who died," Mazzoli said, "one of an OxyContin overdose, and one of a heroin overdose after becoming addicted via Oxycontin. And Royce's father passed away and succumbed to his addiction."

With two major operatic premieres, and an upcoming piano concerto commissioned by the New York Philharmonic, Missy Mazzoli is having a moment. "I joke with my partner, everything in my life is happening in this three-week span," she said. "But I'm just really trying to ride the wave and enjoy it."

Mazzoli says, as a young composer, there were unequal expectations in the industry: "With male creators, they're looking for potential. They're like, 'Oh, he has great potential to do this.' But when it come to hiring a woman, they're like, 'Oh, but she hasn't written an opera yet.' And it's like, But she has the potential."

So, ten years ago, Mazzoli co-founded a non-profit organization called Luna Lab, to mentor and provide performance opportunities to teen composers. "I want to inspire future generations to pursue music as a career and to continue to express themselves in this medium," she said.

While Monday's premiere marked Mazzoli's Met debut, it's also a return of sorts. She first came to the Met when she was 18. The only seat she could afford was in the last row of the highest section: "And it was this seat, right here, and I sat here, and it changed my life!"

title: "The Mosquito Bowl" and the human cost of war
summary: Director Peter Berg discusses his new film, the true story of All-American football stars who volunteered for the Marines and fought in the Battle of Okinawa, the last and costliest World War II battle in the Pacific.
story: Okinawa proved to be the last and costliest battle of World War II in the Pacific – and it's a name director Peter Berg wants us all to remember. His new movie, "The Mosquito Bowl," captures that battle. "It is a film that I hope asks us all to look at what we ask of our young men and women," he said.

"The Mosquito Bowl" is based on the book by Buzz Bissinger, who also wrote "Friday Night Lights," which became Berg's breakout movie. But don't let the title fool you – it's not a movie about a football game. "No, it's not; it's a movie about the cost of war, the human cost of war," said Berg.

The human cost of war as told through the true story of four All-American football players who volunteered for the Marines after Pearl Harbor, and reported to boot camp at Parris Island, South Carolina, which is where we interviewed Berg. "They came down here and they joined the Marine Corps, thinking, Hey, we'll go win this thing. We'll go whup some butt and win this thing, like we win our football games," Berg said. "Then they come across an enemy, the Japanese, who are instructed by their emperor, who they believe is a god, to not surrender."

They first encountered the Japanese on a tiny speck of coral called Tarawa. When footage of American dead on the beach at Tarawa reached the United States, the public saw for the first time the human cost of war. It's the first battle sequence in the movie.
"I wanted it to be as hard and as intense as I could possibly make it," Berg said. "I wanted it to feel terrifying, because that's how I believe it was."

Berg's immersive style of filmmaking uses real flame throwers and real explosions. It's also his style of research. For "Friday Night Lights," he spent a season with a high school football team in Texas. For "Lone Survivor," he spent a month with Navy SEALs in Iraq.

He wrote most of the script for "The Mosquito Bowl" on Parris Island. "Just gets into your blood," he said. "And then I carry that, I try to, onto the set. And that's why I don't worry about the marks, I don't care if your jacket looks perfect, I don't care about the lighting; I want the soul."
For Berg, these recruits at Parris Island are the human cost of future wars. "It's a very, very powerful force," he said. "It's a very dangerous group of human beings. And I do feel responsibility."

To understand Berg, you need to understand that his father was a Marine who served during the Korean War. "My father's buried at Arlington," he said. "And I love my father very much. I go to his grave and I have conversations with him now. They're great, because I get to talk, and he has to listen!"

He said he'd already told his father about "The Mosquito Bowl." When asked what he told him, Berg choked up and excused himself. "Very emotional for me," he later explained. "I told him I was sorry that he couldn't see this film. He would have loved this film."

It's named after a football game played on the island of Guadalcanal shortly before the Marines shipped out for Okinawa. "A football game which really, to me, only matters as an opportunity for these young men to remember what's good about life," Berg said.

"That football game was a big event. That was a big deal," said Neal McCallum. Now 99, he hadn't turned 18 yet, but he was there. He'd joined the Marine Corps ten days after his 17th birthday. "I wanted to get in the war and do my part," he said.
McCallum's memory, plus a photo of the opening handshake and a mimeographed program, are all that remain of the game between two Marine regiments, each loaded with college football stars.

"Oh, it was a great game, back and forth, so it was a tie," said McCallum. The final score: 0-0. "They wanted to play again, but the colonel of the 4th Marines said he could not take that chance and hurt his Marines, because he knew we were going into battle soon."

The battle was Okinawa, and Berg, who started out as an actor, plays the commanding general, telling his Marines, "There's nothing I would like more than to tell you it's going to get easier. It's not. I would love to tell you there will be no more casualties, no more deaths. That's not true."

Berg recreated the hellscape of Okinawa in a quarry in Australia, although nothing can recapture the horrors of that 82-day battle. "The casualties on Okinawa [were] just insufferable, and it was a great sacrifice, a big sacrifice," said McCallum. "Of course, these young guys, their lives were ended. They didn't have opportunities like I did. I survived the war."

More than 12,000 Americans were killed, including 15 of the football stars who played in the Mosquito Bowl. And, as Berg shows, the loss of life for Japanese soldiers and the civilians of Okinawa was almost unimaginable.
"How can you forget something like that?" McCullum asked. "It was so intense, you're not going to forget about it."

You might not remember the exact numbers, but Berg has tried hard to make sure you never forget the human cost of war. "I want you to feel like you're going through it," he said. "I want people to say, 'I felt that. I felt it. I didn't think about it, but I felt it.'"

title: Parker Posey: "I have felt in the right place at the right time"
summary: In the 1990s actress Parker Posey was dubbed "The Queen of the Indies." The Emmy-nominated star of "The White Lotus," and the new film "Wild Horse Nine" talks about her Southern upbringing, and how her parents inspired her acting.
story: This was actress Parker Posey's first headshot as a teenager. "How cute is this?" she laughed.
It's been a long time, but I still see this girl. "I'm still that girl, are you kidding?" she said.

I met that girl in 1985, when we were both 16, at the North Carolina School of the Arts in Winston-Salem. "We were serious young performers," she said. It was a decade before Parker Posey became one of the breakout stars of the 1990s independent film heyday.

We met at a loft which was the very first place she stayed on a trip to New York City. But she's very much a product of her Southern upbringing – and the two people she calls the stars of her family. "My dad would take my mom on dates," she said. "They would go to the grocery store, 'cause they didn't have money, and he would make up stories of the people going in and out of the grocery store to make my mom laugh. So, entertain yourself! And if you can't, work on it, you know?"

And that's what Posey has been doing with particular relish throughout her career. Whether the part is big or small, there's always the sense that she's having fun with it, whether it's "Dazed and Confused," "You've Got Mail," "Josie and the Pussycats," or "Scream 3."

Parker Christian Posey and her twin brother were raised in Monroe, Louisiana, and Laurel, Mississippi. Her mother Lynda was a chef, and her late father Chris owned a car dealership. Her Southern roots came in handy for season three of "The White Lotus," where Posey was Emmy-nominated for her portrayal of the pill-popping and much-quoted North Carolina matriarch Victoria Ratliff.

Was any part of that character her mom? "Oh, my God, of course!" she laughed. "It was all the women in my family, and some people that – I mean, I love the drama that the South brings. I remember being in a grocery store and I just thought this woman was hilarious, and she goes, 'Do you have the ROH-maiiiiiine lettuce?' You're just like, Wow! 'ROH-maiiiiiine'!"

Posey spent several of her summers working at her father's car dealership: "I was always imitating people and putting on accents. I liked speaking over the speaker. And I'd say, "Good morning. Chris Posey Chevrolet Nissan. How may I help you? Mike Wally, you're needed on line one. MIKE WALLY, LINE ONE!!!!!!' Every time would be just, like, start with this, and then just start yelling. I laughed."

While attending the acting program at State University of New York in Purchase, Posey was cast as Tess Shelby on "As the World Turns." "I auditioned on a Monday, and by Tuesday I was packing my bags, and Wednesday I was on camera acting on plastic rocks and AstroTurf, and getting all this wonderful help from the great actors that I was working with," she said.

Her first big lead was in the 1995 film "Party Girl." Plum roles in a slew of lower-budget, critically-acclaimed movies followed, such as "Clockwatchers" and "The Daytrippers." That led to a 1997 Time magazine article proclaiming Posey "The Queen of the Indies" – just as the independent film scene itself was going into decline.

So, was that moniker a mixed blessing? "I don't know. Maybe," she said. "When someone's called a name, it's not a great thing. You're labeled and you're in some corner, right? And then you're not that cool anymore. There's something about being on the pedestal that must be knocked down."
Still, she kept on working, notably as part of Christopher Guest's ensemble, in movies like "Waiting for Guffman" and "Best in Show," where pretty much all of the dialogue was improvised.

"Chris saw that people weren't having children anymore; they were having dogs," Posey said. "And then we started seeing kind of the marketing of dogs, and they just seemed to be more prevalent than they had been. And I'm part of that generation. I had a dog that was like my child.""

She's also been getting lots of young fans, "which feels good, because I don't have kids of my own. So, I have these 19- and 20-year-olds coming up, talking about 'Party Girl' or movies that their parents [watched], or 'The Daytrippers,' these independent movies that they're really enjoying. And that feels so good."

Posey is having yet another moment: hosting a new reality show called "The Mob," and starring alongside John Malkovich and longtime friend Sam Rockwell in the movie "Wild Horse Nine." She's in two scenes and, as always, makes them count. "If I like something, it doesn't matter if the part's big or not, if it's resonating for me as a whole," she said, "which 'Wild Horse Nine' just really felt like. It was like a play … as an actor, you enjoy the whole play."

But I wanted to go back to a moment much earlier in her life, when our acting teacher at the North Carolina School of the Arts said this about a teenage Parker Posey: "She's better than she realizes." "She's gonna make it." And also, "She's more beautiful than she knows."

"That's so sweet," she laughed. "I loved my teachers, yeah. I still, oh, now I can't believe now I'm crying! So grateful I had that guidance. But also my family, I had that guidance, too. Like, I feel like my life has been such a path. It's not been easy at all, but I have felt in the right place at the right time."

title: RFK Jr. to ease access to unapproved peptides, draft policy states
summary: Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. took steps Wednesday that could open up access to certain unapproved peptide drugs that are being promoted for wellness.
story: Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. took steps this week that could open up access to certain unapproved peptide drugs that are being promoted for wellness.

In a draft policy filed Wednesday, Kennedy said he had determined that compounding pharmacies could prepare six specific peptides — BPC-157, Epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, Semax, TB-500 — even though they do not have approval from the Food and Drug Administration.
"By allowing limited compounding of the substances addressed in this guidance under appropriate safeguards, the policy provides patients with a more controlled alternative," Kennedy wrote.
Compounding pharmacies mix ingredients to prepare customized medications for individual patients.
Although they are not FDA approved, the six peptides in Kennedy's new policy are often still marketed with health claims.

The Department of Health and Human Services "did not intend to take action" against licensed pharmacies or physicians that compound "a drug product using a peptide bulk drug substance that is not a component of an FDA-approved drug product," Kennedy's policy said.

Peptides are small proteins that can have powerful effects. There are several, such as insulin, that are FDA approved as being safe and effective. GLP-1 medications used for weight loss and to treat diabetes also contain FDA approved peptides.

In July, an FDA advisory panel voted to recommend allowing the six unapproved peptides to be used in compounding, although that decision did not constitute FDA approval. That vote, however, went against the recommendations of the FDA's own scientists, who said there isn't enough evidence of safety and effectiveness for each of the six peptides to make such a determination.
Kennedy cited that panel's recommendation in his decision, saying he had determined the policy "advances patient choice and freedom while appropriately protecting patient safety."

In a statement provided to CBS News, an HHS spokesperson said that pharmacies will have to do quality testing and safety reporting, and that should help patients know what is in these peptide drugs that are currently being sold by unregulated sources.

"The policy does not grant FDA approval or establish clinical safety and effectiveness," the HHS spokesperson said. "It requires patient-specific prescriptions, traceable ingredients, quality testing, and safety reporting to hold compounders accountable and give patients an alternative to unregulated sellers."
The draft policy requires an FDA-registered ingredient maker, a lab certificate for the raw ingredients, and reports of serious side effects.

In a CBS News investigation published last week, a laboratory test was conducted on an experimental peptide weight-loss drug known as retatrutide that was purchased from a bodega in Brooklyn, New York.
The lab test, however, found that the sample of retatrutide purchased from the bodega did not contain a peptide at all.

A CBS News investigation last summer found that dozens of clinics across the country, staffed by licensed physicians and nurse practitioners, have been openly advertising retatrutide even though it has not been reviewed by the FDA and remains in clinical trials by drug giant Eli Lilly.

Kennedy's draft policy will be open to public comment beginning Friday through Nov. 13. The policy will remain in place until the FDA finalizes a rule regarding compounded peptides. However, at this point, the FDA has not proposed one.
