title: Country star Cody Johnson says Nashville wanted to change him before success
summary: Cody Johnson walked away from a Nashville record deal after executives told him to ditch his cowboy hat, then spent a decade proving them wrong.
story: Cody Johnson talked to Fox News Digital on the iHeartRadio Music Awards carpet, and admitted his pre-show ritual is "pretty simple."
Nashville wanted Cody Johnson to ditch his cowboy hat before giving him a shot at country music stardom.

The Texas-born country star said he walked away from a record deal after executives suggested he swap his signature cowboy look for a baseball cap — a move he viewed as a demand to change who he was before he could make it in the music business.

"They wanted a baseball cap, which I have nothing against, but it was the approach. It was the 'you're great, but once we change you, you'll make it.' And it pissed me off," he said in an interview with "CBS Mornings." "I tipped my hat and said, 'Thank you for your time.'"
CARRIE UNDERWOOD SAYS HER FAMILY COULD BE 'SELF-SUSTAINED' ON TENNESSEE FARM AWAY FROM HOLLYWOOD SPOTLIGHT
Cody Johnson performs onstage during the 61st Academy of Country Music Awards at MGM Grand Garden Arena in Las Vegas, on May 17, 2026. (John Shearer/Getty Images for ACM)
It was a gamble that could have cost him his shot at stardom.
Instead, Johnson spent the next 10 years building a career on his own terms, playing bars and honky-tonks before becoming one of country music's biggest stars.
During his interview, Johnson spoke candidly about his rise to fame and the years of work behind his success.
COUNTRY SINGER CODY JOHNSON FORCED TO STOP 'GOD BLESS AMERICA' PERFORMANCE AS VIOLENT BRAWL BREAKS OUT
Long before arena crowds and industry recognition, the singer was a small-town Texas kid who dreamed of becoming a rodeo star.

Country music star Cody Johnson revealed he walked away from a Nashville record-label opportunity after executives pushed him to trade his signature cowboy hat for a baseball cap. (Mary DeCicco/MLB Photos via Getty Images)
He eventually traded bull riding for music after years of injuries and setbacks and selling CDs in rodeo parking lots as he tried to build a following.
The country star also struggled to believe his ambitions were within reach.
THOMAS RHETT REVEALS WHY HE AND WIFE LAUREN REJECT CELEBRITY PERKS FOR COUNTRY LIFE
"Truthfully, in my core, I didn't feel I was capable of attaining a goal that big, you know, to be a huge country music star, to own a cattle ranch," Johnson said.
Cody Johnson refused to compromise his cowboy image to satisfy Nashville executives, choosing to build his country music career on his own terms. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)
After turning down the label opportunity, he spent years playing small venues, struggling financially and spending long stretches away from his family to keep his career alive.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"The pressure of knowing that you don't know how to pay your water bill, and you've just been on the road for a month and haven't seen your wife or your child, and you have nothing to show for it. That's that's tough to look in the mirror."

Country singer Cody Johnson spent a decade performing in bars and honky-tonks before achieving mainstream success without abandoning his traditional cowboy style. (Christopher Polk/Dick Clark Productions via Getty Images)
He continued, "I think that I just had decided at that point that no matter what, no matter how hard, no matter how high the mountain, I will not back down. I will not quit."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
After a decade of grinding it out as an independent artist, Johnson saw record labels return with another opportunity — this time, he said, without the same demand to change his image.
"I just get to be myself and be authentic," he said.

Johnson has built a national following, sold out arenas and earned a place among country music's leading performers, while keeping the cowboy image he refused to abandon.

title: Rob Lowe gets candid about his best on-screen kiss as other major stars dish on their worst
summary: Rob Lowe called Nastassja Kinski his best on-screen kiss, while Nicole Kidman roasted Alexander Skarsgard over a falafel-fueled smooch scene.
story: During an appearance on "Nostalgia Tonight with Joe Sibilia," the "Seinfeld" star recalls filming romantic scenes with Carol Burnett, revealing the actress's playful joke. He also reflects on other unforgettable TV legends.
Celebrities are getting real about their best and worst on-screen smooches.
Rob Lowe recently praised one of his former co-stars as the best on-screen kiss of his career, while Nicole Kidman previously roasted one of her former screen partners as her worst.
Whether it was the circumstances surrounding the shoot, the chemistry between the actors or a co-star's choices at lunch, these star's share what can make or break a romantic scene for them.
Here are some stars who have disclosed their best and worst on-screen kisses.
Rob Lowe
Lowe said Nastassja Kinski was his best on-screen kiss. (Clark Clifford/The Hollywood Reporter via Getty Images)
Rob Lowe dished on the actress he considers to be his best on-screen kiss.

During a recent appearance on "Watch What Happens Live," the "The Outsiders" star told host Andy Cohen while playing "Plead the Fifth" that his best kiss was with co-star, Nastassja Kinski, while filming "The Hotel New Hampshire."
"Have a look at her," he said when asked what made her the best. "At that moment in time, she was probably the most beautiful woman I’d certainly ever seen."
While she was his favorite co-star to kiss, he also mentioned he felt "very, very scared" to kiss her.
Sharon Stone
Robert De Niro and Sharon Stone having a tender moment as they lay on a bed in a scene from the film 'Casino', 1995. (Photo by Universal Pictures/Getty Images) (Universal Pictures/Getty Images)
Sharon Stone has only one co-star in mind when it comes to her best kiss.

During an interview on  SiriusXM’s "Radio Andy" in April, the actress called Robert De Niro, "the best kisser in the business," and said the kiss they shared while filming the 1995 movie, "Chicago," "really just knocked me out."

"We did this scene where I have to go to the bathroom, and because I play this hustler, I get him to give me money to go," Stone explained. "He gives me this money and I look at him like, ‘Really? I think a little more than $50 for the bathroom.' And he … reaches in, and he gives me, like, $100, and then I lean over, and I kiss him."
ROBERT DE NIRO GETS EMOTIONAL AS AMY POEHLER PRAISES HIM FOR SPEAKING 'TRUTH TO POWER' AS REGULAR TRUMP CRITIC

The kiss was enjoyed by both her and De Niro, with Stone telling Andy Cohen that when director, Martin Scorsese, asked if they wanted to film the scene again, "We both looked at him and went, 'Yeah, I think maybe we need one more.'"
Sylvester Stallone
Stallone said his kiss with Talia Shire was the worst in his career. (Sunset Boulevard/Corbis via Getty Images)
Although fans love the kiss between Rocky Balboa and Adrian in "Rocky," Sylvester Stallone doesn't have fond memories from filming the scene.
In a recent interview with Page Six Hollywood, Stallone referred to his kiss with actress Talia Shire as "the kiss from hell," but it was no fault of the actress.

And I go, ‘Oh my God!’And I have to keep moving forward. There is no reverse. So I knew exactly as soon as I kissed her that within an hour I had the flu."

Kidman said Skarsgard is her worst on-screen kiss because he ate falafel before filming the scene. (Dan MacMedan/Getty Images)

title: Date-rape drug at center of Cornell sex assault allegations can leave victims unaware of surroundings
summary: A former Cornell University student described feeling severe dissociation after taking ketamine before an alleged fraternity gang rape as Dr. Stephanie Widner shared insights.
story: Fox News contributor Dr. Stephanie Widmer explains the dangerous effects of ketamine, including sedation, memory loss and dissociation, and warns parents about the risks of drug use on college campuses.

An investigation into an alleged gang rape at a Cornell University fraternity has thrust the illicit use of ketamine into the spotlight, calling attention to the powerful anesthetic’s use on college campuses as a date-rape drug.
A former Cornell student testified before the university’s hearing panel that ketamine made her feel "like her lights were on but no one was home," describing a state of "vague consciousness."

During an appearance on "Fox & Friends" on Wednesday, Oct. 28, Dr. Stephanie Widmer, a Fox News contributor and addiction specialist in New York, warned that the drug’s physiological effects can leave people unable to defend themselves or understand their environment.
INSIDE EXPLOSIVE CORNELL RAPE ALLEGATIONS: 7 MEN ACCUSED, CONFLICTING ACCOUNTS AND A POLITICAL FIRESTORM
"When you say the lights are on, but nobody’s home, that’s a pretty good way to describe it," Widmer said.
"You can essentially have no awareness of your surroundings."
The fraternity house at the center of a rape allegation is shown on the campus of Cornell University on Oct. 8, 2026, in Ithaca, New York. (Ryan Murphy/Getty Images)
Ketamine affects NMDA receptors in the brain and can alter vital signs, according to the doctor.
"It can cause profound sedation, and it can cause dissociation, which is essentially the sensation of your brain not really being attached to your body," she said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

While ketamine has legitimate medical uses — it was used as a battlefield anesthetic during the Vietnam War and remains FDA-approved for general anesthesia — the drug is also abused recreationally at parties, raves and nightclubs.
Due to its ability to induce heavy sedation, impair decision-making and disrupt memory, ketamine is categorized and exploited as a date rape drug. (iStock)

The Drug Enforcement Administration classifies ketamine as a Schedule III controlled substance and identifies it, alongside Rohypnol and GHB, as a drug that can be used to facilitate sexual assault. The agency says these substances can cause sedation, confusion and memory loss, leaving victims vulnerable.
When asked why ketamine falls into the category of date-rape drugs, Widmer said it can affect both cognitive function and physical awareness.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"There are a number of date-rape drugs that are out there, and ketamine does fall into that category because of what it can do to your sensorium," she added.
While ketamine has legitimate medical applications, its illicit recreational misuse poses serious safety hazards, experts warn. (iStock)
Widmer also warned about mixing ketamine with alcohol or other substances, which can compound the drugs’ effects and increase the risk of dangerous sedation and respiratory depression.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"They’re combining them with other substances, they’re combining them with alcohol, and that can compound the effects of these drugs," she said.
"It can cause really profound sedation. It can be incredibly dangerous."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Widmer said her biggest concern is how parents discuss the dangers of drugs with their children, especially before sending them off to college.

"Everybody knows to say drugs are bad and not to do drugs, and you never know what you’re getting, but really understanding what some of these drugs can do is really important. … They’re not benign and they can cause dissociation."

title: Weight-loss drug could help address nighttime sleep disruptions for millions
summary: Eli Lilly's retatrutide cut breathing interruptions and drove significant weight loss in sleep apnea patients, as well as cardiovascular benefits.
story: Cardiologist Dr. Virend Somers discusses how the weight-loss drug retatrutide significantly reduced obstructive sleep apnea severity and improved cardiovascular risk factors in patients with and without type 2 diabetes.

An experimental obesity drug significantly reduced breathing interruptions and other symptoms of obstructive sleep disorder in two clinical trials, according to new research published in The New England Journal of Medicine.
Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) affects more than 50 million Americans, and about 80% of cases are undiagnosed, according to the National Sleep Foundation.
The study examined whether retatrutide, an investigational weight-loss drug from Eli Lilly, could help treat OSA in adults who were overweight or obese.
EXPERIMENTAL OBESITY DRUG OUTPERFORMS TRADITIONAL WEIGHT-LOSS TREATMENTS IN EARLY RESEARCH
Retatrutide is being evaluated in phase 3 TRIUMPH trials as a potential treatment for obesity and related metabolic conditions. The drug has not been approved by the FDA.
The FDA has warned that unauthorized versions of retatrutide have been illegally marketed and sold online for weight loss.
The researchers measured changes in the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI), which counts breathing interruptions per hour of sleep. (iStock)
Study details

The two phase 3 randomized trials included 691 adults with moderate-to-severe sleep apnea and a BMI of at least 27. Participants received once-weekly injections of retatrutide at doses of 4, 9 or 12 milligrams, or a placebo, and were followed for 80 weeks.
The trials included 243 participants without type 2 diabetes and 448 with the condition.
WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY FIGHT 7 SERIOUS HEALTH PROBLEMS BEFORE THE POUNDS EVEN COME OFF
Participants who received retatrutide lost between 12% and nearly 20% of their body weight and experienced significantly fewer breathing interruptions than those who received a placebo.
About 68% of participants experienced more than a 50% improvement in OSA symptoms, regardless of whether they had type 2 diabetes.
Retatrutide improved more than 50% of OSA symptoms in 68% of participants over the 80-week period. (iStock)

The study also found that hypoxic burden — the severity and duration of low-oxygen episodes caused by breathing disruptions during sleep — fell by about 75% among participants without type 2 diabetes and 65% among those with the condition.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

The researchers concluded that retatrutide led to significantly greater reductions in AHI (breathing interruptions) than a placebo among adults with OSA who were obese or overweight, regardless of whether they had type 2 diabetes.
The need for CPAP machines could be reduced by drug therapy, the researchers considered. (iStock)
The researchers noted that retatrutide’s lack of FDA approval was a limitation, and further studies are needed to determine how the drug may affect long-term cardiovascular outcomes.
Expert reaction

Study co-author Dr. Virend Somers, a cardiologist and professor of medicine at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, told Fox News Digital that while the results were expected, he was surprised by the "magnitude of benefit in patients with type 2 diabetes," as well as the significant reduction in sleep apnea.
"OSA is often under-diagnosed and under-treated."
"This is a very exciting time in treating sleep apnea patients," Somers said.

Sleep apnea is associated with a higher risk of heart attacks, strokes, high blood pressure and atrial fibrillation. In the trial, participants experienced reductions in several cardiovascular risk factors, including systolic blood pressure, LDL cholesterol, systemic inflammation and neck circumference.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"A reduction in these measures would predict whether these patients were at increased cardiovascular risk," Somers told Fox News Digital.
"In diabetics, blood pressure is a key determinant of future cardiovascular risk, and the fact that we were able to reduce it so significantly was both surprising and exciting."
Sleep apnea patients are at higher risk for heart attacks, strokes, high blood pressure and atrial fibrillation. (iStock)
Somers said retatrutide also improved several diabetes-related measures.

In participants without diabetes, insulin levels fell by more than 50%. Among those with type 2 diabetes, 40% progressed from diabetes to prediabetes and another 40% no longer met the criteria for diabetes, according to the researcher.
The improvements were largely linked to weight loss, which can lead to better sleep and reduced sleep-related impairment, he said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"[The participants] reported much improved sleep beyond just the sleep apnea — what we call sleep-related impairment was significantly reduced," Somers said.

The study included participants who were using CPAP and those who were not. Somers said CPAP use generally declined during the study, suggesting that some patients may eventually require less device-based treatment.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Dr. Wendy Troxel, a RAND senior behavioral scientist in Utah who was not involved in the study, noted that OSA is often under-diagnosed and under-treated, especially among postmenopausal women.

"Although CPAP remains the frontline treatment for sleep apnea, my hope is that greater awareness of treatment options may encourage more people to get screened and seek treatment," she told Fox News Digital.
Somers noted that the condition completely resolved in about 25% of participants without diabetes and 15% of those with type 2 diabetes.
"This is a very exciting time in treating sleep apnea patients."

The study’s findings do not mean patients should stop using CPAP or other prescribed treatments, the researchers emphasized. Additional research is needed to determine retatrutide's long-term safety and effectiveness for sleep apnea.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"There’s hope on the horizon," Somers said. "We have the CPAP, we have mandibular devices, we have postural therapy, where you try to avoid sleeping on your back, and now we’ve got drug therapies that can potentially not just reduce your apnea, but also make you sleep better ... and reduce the risk of future cardiovascular events."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Simple exercise done just once a week could help lower blood pressure
summary: Isometric exercise training like home wall squats produced significant blood pressure drops, but a cardiologist says dietary change may matter even more.
story: Tom Shillue discusses a new sprinting study on 'Gutfeld!' showing three minutes of intense exercise beats hours of moderate cardio. Former Navy SEAL Rob O'Neill and Kat Timpf react with their own workout routines.
Holding a wall squat for a few minutes might not feel like an intense workout, but a growing body of evidence suggests it could be one of the most effective ways to lower your blood pressure.

A trial published in BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine found that isometric exercise training, where muscles contract without moving the joints, leads to meaningful drops in resting blood pressure within just four weeks.
Researchers also found that daily exercise may not be necessary to maintain these benefits, as exercising just once a week was enough to preserve some heart-health improvements.
ANCIENT CHINESE MOVEMENT SHOWS PROMISE FOR REDUCING BLOOD PRESSURE AT HOME, STUDY SAYS
The study followed 100 inactive adults with normal to high-normal blood pressure, defined as a systolic reading between 120 and 140 millimeters of mercury.

For the first four weeks, the participants performed lower-body isometric wall squats three times a week at home. The routine consisted of four two-minute sessions separated by two minutes of seated rest, monitored using heart-rate straps to ensure consistent effort.
The study followed 100 inactive adults with normal to high-normal blood pressure, defined as a systolic reading between 120 and 140 millimeters of mercury. (iStock)

After four weeks, participants’ top blood pressure number (systolic pressure) fell by about 9.5 points on average, while their bottom number (diastolic pressure) also dropped compared with the control group.
Researchers then examined the effects of reduced exercise frequency. During the following four weeks, participants were randomly assigned to train three, two, one or zero times per week.
EVERYDAY HABIT LINKED TO DRAMATICALLY LOWER RISK OF DYING FROM HEART DISEASE
Those who stopped exercising completely saw their blood pressure bounce back to baseline within four weeks, essentially wiping out their progress.
In contrast, participants who kept training just once or twice a week managed to hold onto a significant portion of their blood pressure reductions.
Participants who kept training just once or twice a week managed to hold onto a significant portion of their blood pressure reductions. (iStock)
Only the group that continued training three times weekly retained key improvements in the following metrics.

Total peripheral resistance, which measures the resistance blood encounters as it flows through the vesselsHeart rate variability, the variation in time between heartbeatsReflex sensitivity, which reflects how efficiently the nervous system regulates blood pressure beat by beat

"This is a fascinating study revealing just a little bit of the right exercise even once a week has likely demonstrable cardiovascular benefits in terms of blood pressure reduction," Dr. Aseem Malhotra, a cardiologist and metabolic health specialist at Ovadia Heart Health in Florida, told Fox News Digital.
"It also doesn’t cost anything to do wall squats at home."
Isometric wall squats performed three times weekly produced significant drops in resting blood pressure in just four weeks. (iStock)
Malhotra, who was not involved in the study, noted that physical movement is only one piece of the puzzle.
"In my own personal clinical practice, I regularly see significant improvements in blood pressure with many patients coming off medication just from dietary change alone," he said.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"A low-carb Mediterranean diet is, in my view, the most substantial and effective intervention – not just for blood pressure, but for all metabolic health markers."
Completely stopping the isometric routine caused blood pressure levels to rebound quickly back to their original baseline. (andreswd / Getty Images)
The study cohort was relatively modest in size, consisting of 100 generally healthy, non-smoking adults who were not taking blood pressure medications.

The findings cannot automatically be generalized to individuals with diagnosed hypertension, older populations with mobility limitations, or patients who are already on heart medications, the researchers acknowledged.

Additionally, because the maintenance phase lasted only four weeks, the researchers noted that longer-term trials are needed to see whether a once-weekly session can sustain blood pressure reductions over months or years.
Because the study involved physical activity, participants and researchers knew each person’s assigned exercise group.

title: Blood sugar spikes may be tied to everyday habits you can control, expert says
summary: Jim LaValle reveals how post-meal glucose spikes, insulin resistance and sleep apnea are deeply connected, plus the 10-minute walking habit.
story: Metabolic health expert Jim LaValle explains how chronic stress, inadequate sleep and everyday dietary choices can affect blood sugar regulation and contribute to insulin resistance.
Everyday habits — from what you eat for breakfast to how much you sleep — can have a significant impact on blood sugar levels, according to a metabolic health expert.
Maintaining healthy blood sugar levels is essential for energy, organ function and overall metabolic health, while frequent or prolonged spikes and drops can contribute to health complications.

Jim LaValle, a Texas-based clinical pharmacist and metabolic medicine expert, told Fox News Digital that understanding how food, exercise, sleep and stress affect blood sugar is key to keeping levels in check.
POPULAR DIET SLASHES LIVER FAT BY 67% WHILE REVERSING PREDIABETES IN SOME PEOPLE
LaValle recommends monitoring blood sugar after meals, known as postprandial glucose, to better understand how different foods, beverages and eating habits affect blood sugar levels.
"Do I spike more from eating rice, or do I spike from eating quinoa? How much can I eat?" he said. "I think that's a foundational issue."
Stable glucose levels are essential for energy, organ function and overall metabolic balance, while spikes and drops can contribute to long-term health effects. (iStock)
The metabolic health expert noted that insulin resistance occurs when cells become less responsive to insulin, a process that can be influenced by inflammation in the body.
Normally, insulin helps move glucose from the bloodstream into muscle cells, where it can be stored as glycogen for later use.
THINK YOUR CORTISOL IS TOO HIGH? EXPERT REVEALS THE TRUTH BEHIND VIRAL WELLNESS CRAZE

LaValle said he’s a "big believer" in eating a higher-protein breakfast rather than one that’s heavy in carbs, pointing to naturally elevated cortisol levels in the morning and their potential impact on blood sugar.
"You've got to watch how many sugars are in food, how many refined carbohydrates you're [eating]," he added.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

One of the simplest lifestyle habits to help lower blood sugar, according to LaValle, is taking a 10-minute walk after eating. Regular exercise is an "obvious" healthy practice, he added, although he acknowledged that it's not easy for everyone.
The expert recommends taking a 10-minute walk after eating to balance blood sugar levels. (iStock)

"It’s easy to say, ‘eat better, exercise, sleep better,’ but then people are working 16-hour days or are single parents, they get home, they open up their pantry and destroy a bag of cookies because that's the first thing they can eat and their blood sugar’s plummeted," he said.
Even a little movement after eating can be beneficial, LaValle said, particularly in a modern world that’s "eliminating the need to move."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
LaValle also emphasized the importance of managing stress, which can contribute to insulin resistance.
Along with healthy eating, exercise and stress management, getting adequate sleep is "huge for glucose regulation," he added.
"You've got to watch how many sugars are in food, how many refined carbohydrates you're [eating]," the expert advised. (iStock)

"When you don't sleep, and you don’t get enough rest to reset your body for the next day ... all those hormones that are supposed to be getting released get skewed," LaValle said, noting that insulin regulation is particularly affected by inadequate sleep.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
LaValle noted that sleep apnea is often associated with conditions such as diabetes, prediabetes, high blood pressure and obesity, emphasizing the importance of healthy sleep habits.
Hyperarousal of the brain can contribute to insomnia, LaValle added.
Sleep hygiene is important for keeping weight and stress in check, the expert said. (iStock)
For someone who’s "jacked up all day long," feeling overcommitted and anxious, that heightened state of stress can disrupt sleep and, in turn, interfere with glucose regulation.
Inadequate sleep can also affect appetite and eating behaviors, potentially making blood sugar management more difficult.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Then you're going to start to put weight on and then, when you don't get enough sleep, you’ve got to eat more to fuel your brain," LaValle cautioned.
"So you eat more, you're not efficient at packaging that fuel up, you're moving less ... and those are the things that you have control over."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Diagnostic test could flag which men need aggressive prostate cancer treatment and which don't
summary: The Decipher genomic test could help doctors decide which high-risk prostate cancer patients need abiraterone hormone therapy and which can skip it.
story: Musician Wayne Singleton shares how a routine physical led to a rare prostate cancer diagnosis at 33 years old, and encourages others to prioritize regular health checks.
A new diagnostic test could improve the prostate cancer experience for millions of men.

Researchers at University College London (UCL) analyzed a tissue-based molecular test called Decipher to determine which men with high-risk prostate cancer were most likely to benefit from stronger treatment — and which might avoid unnecessary medication and side effects.
The analysis focused on abiraterone, a hormone therapy that was shown in the STAMPEDE clinical trial to cut the risk of death in half among men with high-risk, localized prostate cancer.
JOE BIDEN SHARES HEALTH UPDATE AFTER PROSTATE CANCER DIAGNOSIS WHILE ISSUING WARNING TO OTHERS
The findings were presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) Congress 2026 in Madrid, held Oct. 23–27.
Not every cancer is alike, and treating someone more aggressively than necessary could have "increased side effects and poorer quality of life," noted a UCL news release.
Adding a hormone therapy called abiraterone to standard treatment for men with high-risk, localized prostate cancer could cut the risk of death in half, the trial found.
Because prostate cancers differ at the molecular level, not every patient benefits from adding hormone therapy.

To determine whether Decipher could help guide that decision, researchers examined test scores from more than 27,000 patients in real-world data and 401 men with non-metastatic prostate cancer who had participated in the STAMPEDE abiraterone trial.
PATIENTS REMAIN CANCER-FREE NEARLY 3 YEARS AFTER RECEIVING EXPERIMENTAL IMMUNOTHERAPY

Higher Decipher scores predicted worse outcomes, meaning the cancer is more likely to spread and additional treatment may be valuable. A low Decipher score suggested more intensive treatment may be unnecessary.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Lead researcher Dr. Sarah Howlett of UCL Cancer Institute commented in a statement that for men with very high-risk prostate cancer, preventing spread of the disease is "critical."
"Understanding who benefits most from additional treatment can make a meaningful difference," she added.
A genomic test could help to personalize treatments for prostate cancer patients, the researchers suggested. (iStock)
The findings suggest that genomic testing could help tailor treatment, according to the researcher.

Men with high-risk prostate cancer and low Decipher scores may face a lower risk of spread and could avoid more intensive therapy, while those with high scores may be the strongest candidates for additional treatment.
Identifying the same pattern in both a large, real-world dataset and a randomized clinical trial strengthens the findings, Howlett noted.
CANCER WARNING SIGNS MAY APPEAR IN DNA YEARS BEFORE BLOOD TESTS DETECT TROUBLE
"But further validation in other datasets is needed before the test is used routinely to make these decisions," she said.

Elai Davicioni, medical director of urology for Decipher test maker Veracyte, also commented, "We believe this growing evidence gives physicians a stronger reason to use Decipher before making decisions that can affect both cancer outcomes and patients’ quality of life."

Men with high-risk prostate cancer and low Decipher scores may face a lower risk of spread and could avoid more intensive therapy, while those with high scores may be the strongest candidates for additional treatment. (iStock)
Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel, who was not involved in the study, also commented on the findings.
"Prostate cancer varies from person to person," he said. "Medical science is increasingly aware that it is not one size fits all."
Localized prostate cancer, which has not yet spread, may contain mutations that predict how aggressive the disease will be and indicate whether it could respond to targeted therapies, Siegel noted.
About one in eight American men will be diagnosed with prostate cancer in their lifetime, according to the American Cancer Society. (iStock)

Certain targeted therapies are being used more with widespread prostate cancer, according to the doctor, as they include "more powerful anti-androgens, which works not just on the testes, but on the adrenals as well."
Hormone therapies have "significant side effects," including fatigue, and "don’t always help," he added.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Siegel said the study’s strength was its combination of a randomized treatment group with Decipher testing, which helped identify in advance which patients were most likely to respond to intensive hormone therapy.
"This is the personalized, precise approach of the near future," he said.
Many men, but not all with high-risk localized prostate cancer, will have a cancer recurrence after local therapy, according to the doctor. (Getty Images )
Dr. William Dahut, M.D., chief scientific officer at the American Cancer Society, noted that many men with high-risk localized prostate cancer will have a recurrence after local therapy.

"This study shows that by combining drugs that interfere with the male hormone testosterone with standard therapy, the risk of cancer recurrence decreases," the Maryland-based doctor, who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Traditionally, if a more intensive therapy benefits some patients, it is offered to all men — even though only a subset may actually benefit, according to Dahut.

"However, a diagnostic test can greatly improve the treatment experience for a patient by potentially only subjecting patients to more intensive therapies whose genomic test predicts the greatest risk of recurrence," he said.
Dahut encouraged patients to speak with their doctors about intensive therapy to decrease the risk of cancer recurrence, as well as to ask about available genomic testing.

The doctor noted that since the study was conducted with a drug to block testosterone and the oral drug abiraterone, it's "unclear whether the Decipher test would be as accurate with other possible combinations that a patient might receive."

Prostate cancer is the second-leading cause of cancer death behind lung cancer, according to the American Cancer Society. About one in eight American men will be diagnosed with prostate cancer in their lifetime.

title: People living past 100 in one tiny village share 3 daily habits
summary: National Geographic's potential blue zone in Sardinia's Bolotana has 10 centenarians among 2,262 residents, and their plant-based diet holds secrets.
story: Blue Zones Founder Dan Buettner explores why women in a small Italian village are reaching age 100 at remarkable rates, highlighting the importance of friendships, shared responsibilities and everyday movement.
National Geographic researchers believe they may have discovered a new "blue zone."

A blue zone is a geographic region where residents show unusually high rates of longevity and survival into old age. The newest blue zone candidate is a small village called Bolotana, located on the Italian island of Sardinia.
In a 2024 snapshot, 10 of the village's 2,262 residents were at least 100 years old, according to National Geographic — roughly 10 times the Sardinian average and 11 times the U.S. average.
PEOPLE WHO LIVE TO 100 HAVE 3 DRINKS IN COMMON, LONGEVITY EXPERT SAYS
A team of researchers, including Dan Buettner — founder of Blue Zones, a company focused on longevity, and a National Geographic Fellow — set out to investigate Bolotana’s exceptional lifespan.
The findings were published in Frontiers in Aging.
Bolotana’s hilly streets encourage residents to walk as part of their daily routines. (Marisa Montibeller)
Buettner highlighted three lifestyle habits that are common among Bolotana’s long-lived residents.
They move throughout the day: Residents walk steep streets to shops, cafés, workplaces and friends’ homes.
They eat a largely plant-based diet: Beans, vegetables, wheat, olives and olive oil are traditional staples.
They stay socially connected: Residents regularly gather with friends, family and neighbors through meals, church and community activities.
"Here, men are participating more, and that could explain why women are doing better."
The study did not establish that these habits directly cause longevity, but researchers are examining how the village’s environment and traditions may contribute to its unusually high survival rates.

"The international team of demographers, their population scientists … were able to examine the birth records, death records and baptismal records and see that this is probably the richest, most complete data on centenarians in the world," Buettner told Fox News Digital.
AMERICA'S LIFESPAN HAS DOUBLED SINCE 1776 — EXPERTS REVEAL WHAT CHANGED
"For those of us who want to make it into our 90s and 100s in full health, this place does it better than anyplace else in the world."
The strongest longevity advantage appeared among Bolotana’s women, who ranked second only to Hong Kong for life expectancy at age 70 and survival from age 70 to 100.
Bolotana, Sardinia, is home to ancient olive groves. (Marisa Montibeller)
What sets Bolotana apart

The original Sardinian blue zone was identified in the late 1990s and formally described in research published around 2000. Located in the mountainous region roughly 68 miles from Bolotana, it is known for unusually strong male longevity, according to Buettner.

Although Bolotana remains partly pastoral, it is also an agricultural community. Buettner suggested that this may mean men spend more time at home helping with household responsibilities, potentially reducing the burden on women.
Dan Buettner, middle, is pictured with two centenarian women of Bolotana. (Marisa Montibeller)

"In the original blue zone in the highlands, the [women] worried about the finances and raising children and the leaky roof," he said. "They're all alone. Here, men are participating more, and that could explain why women are doing better, because they're only bearing half the stress load instead of almost all of it."
Buettner believes the village’s strong social connections may be one factor behind the women’s longevity, although the study did not establish a cause.
GEORGIA WOMAN CELEBRATES 112TH BIRTHDAY, REVEALS HER SECRET TO A LONG LIFE

"We see women gathering in the library, baking bread together, making sweets together and going to church together," he said. "So, you see a much more socially connected society among the women in Bolotana than in the other blue zones."
As in many parts of Italy, Bolotana has a strong Catholic tradition. Buettner said church attendance may provide residents with faith, social connection and a sense of belonging.
Bolotana church culture connects its residents to faith and to each other. (Marisa Montibeller)

"It’s a sense of community, but it's also people proactively understanding that sitting down with a friend and talking about your troubles and your day with somebody who cares about you is a much more powerful drug than a pharmaceutical," Buettner said.
"The human species has shown this over and over, and Bolotana is a perfect example."
The Bolotana diet
Diet varies among blue zones, but Bolotana’s traditional fare is largely plant-based, with a focus on beans, vegetables, wheat, olives and olive oil, along with some cheese and meat.
DOCTOR'S 10 RULES FOR LIVING LONGER, CELEBRATING MORE BIRTHDAYS AND MAKING EXTRA YEARS COUNT
"About 90% of a centenarian's diet has been all plant-based," Buettner said. "Not protein, by the way. These aren't protein loaders. These are complex carbohydrate loaders."
Dan Buettner prepares a traditional minestrone with Anna Maria Filia in Bolotana. (Marisa Montibeller)

A Bolotanese breakfast might consist of a piece of bread or cheese with local olives and a cup of coffee. Lunch, the biggest meal of the day that starts in the early afternoon, is "almost always" a minestrone soup made with locally grown seasonal vegetables and lots of beans.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"Beans are the cornerstone of the longevity diet here," Buettner said. "Garbanzo beans, lentil beans, pinto beans, cannellini beans — these are really the all-star of the diet."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Traditionally, residents ate meat about five times per month, usually as a celebratory food.
In the highlands, people traditionally cooked with lard, Buettner said, while Bolotana residents use olive oil from ancient trees.

Giaccomo Nieddu maintains an ancient olive grove in Bolotana. The oil contains unusually high levels of odd-chain fatty acids, which researchers are studying for possible links to longevity. (Marisa Montibeller)
Researchers are studying whether the oil’s unusually high levels of odd-chain fatty acids could be relevant to longevity.
‘Not chasing’ longevity
Bolotana residents are not deliberately pursuing longer lives, the longevity researcher noted. The region has little emphasis on gym culture or biohacking.
"These are real humans with an average set of genes," Buettner said. "These aren’t superhumans with superhuman discipline or better genes."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"They’re not chasing longevity," he added. "It is the product of their environment."
Because Bolotana’s streets are steep and residents rarely drive within town, they typically walk to shops, cafés, workplaces and friends’ homes, Buettner said.
"It’s this sort of unconscious walking that’s far more important for longevity than going to the gym."
Bolotana residents walk steep hills for everyday tasks and socialize regularly. (Marisa Montibeller)
Buettner said Bolotana is an example of how daily routines and surroundings can encourage movement without requiring residents to schedule formal exercise.
Residents of walkable American communities have a three- to five-year life-expectancy advantage over those in less-walkable areas, he said.
Centenarians Salvatore and Nina spend time socializing daily in Bolotana. (Marisa Montibeller)

"If we want a healthier America, we have to start thinking about shaping our neighborhoods and our cities so people can unconsciously move and not rely on heaping another obligation on their busy lives to remember to go to the gym," the expert said.

"Most of the things that lead to Bolotana longevity are also pleasant and make the journey a joy," he added.

title: Sharpen memory and fight brain fog with simple 60-second trick from a neurologist
summary: Dr. Rhonda Voskuhl explains why crosswords and sudoku miss the mark for brain fog and which timed word games actually target verbal memory loss.
story: Estrogen loss during menopause can affect verbal memory, processing speed and focus. A neurologist shares why targeted brain exercises may be more helpful than random cognitive games for addressing specific challenges.
Brain games, crosswords and math puzzles are often promoted as ways to sharpen memory, but neurologists warn that generic exercises may not address the specific cause of mental fog.
Dr. Rhonda Voskuhl, a professor of neurology at UCLA and co-founder of Cleopatra RX in Los Angeles, says brain exercises only work if they target the specific mental function that is slowing down.
"You can’t just do random cognitive exercises," Voskuhl told Fox News Digital at the Livelong Women’s Health Summit in New York City in September. "They’ve got to fit the problem."
DOCTOR REVEALS '10-YEAR RULE' FOR EVALUATING BRAIN FOG AND DEMENTIA SYMPTOMS
The problem, she said, is verbal memory. "Doing math is not going to help … You need an exercise that will help you with words."
Generic brain games like Sudoku or number puzzles often fail to clear up mental fog because they do not target the specific brain functions that are slowing down. (iStock)
Mental fog — especially the kind triggered by midlife hormone changes during perimenopause and menopause — impacts very specific areas of the brain, according to Voskuhl.

When estrogen levels drop, overall intelligence and basic logic remain completely normal. Instead, the brain takes a hit in two main areas: verbal memory (recalling names and words) and processing speed (thinking quickly under pressure), experts say.
FORGETTING NAMES AND LOSING KEYS MAY SIGNAL SOMETHING OTHER THAN DEMENTIA
Games like Sudoku and other number puzzles primarily exercise logic and math skills, so they may not improve word-recall difficulties.

"It’s not a global problem with the brain," Voskuhl said. "It’s not global brain atrophy, but there are some regions on MRIs and research studies that show that the hippocampus, the memory area, will have some atrophies, some functional connection issues."
Effective cognitive training must match the person's specific weakness, a neurologist said. (iStock)
To understand why word-based exercises may help, it is useful to distinguish between the following two stages of memory, experts say.
DAILY EATING HABIT LINKED TO BETTER BRAIN HEALTH IN OLDER ADULTS, NEW RESEARCH SUGGESTS
Encoding: How the brain takes in and stores new informationRetrieval: How the brain pulls up that stored information when it's needed
Encoding: How the brain takes in and stores new information
Retrieval: How the brain pulls up that stored information when it's needed
Brain fog typically affects retrieval, not encoding. The word or name is still stored safely in the memory, but the brain's search engine is running slowly.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Building a better brain workout
To effectively target brain fog, Voskuhl says exercises need to focus on two things: finding words and working quickly.
"It’s basically processing speed," she said. "So you need an exercise that is going to be something that makes you rush, makes you do it quickly."
Midlife mental fog from estrogen loss affects localized brain areas tied to verbal memory and processing speed while leaving overall IQ, math logic and general reasoning intact. (iStock)
The following types of exercises target processing speed and active word recall.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Timed word games: Set a 60-second timer to list as many words in a single category as possible (like naming animals or foods).Speed reading and quick summaries: Read a short article quickly, then immediately summarize it out loud in two or three sentences.Rapid recall drills: Use flashcards or picture prompts to name objects or people as fast as possible without pausing.
Timed word games: Set a 60-second timer to list as many words in a single category as possible (like naming animals or foods).
Speed reading and quick summaries: Read a short article quickly, then immediately summarize it out loud in two or three sentences.
Rapid recall drills: Use flashcards or picture prompts to name objects or people as fast as possible without pausing.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Experts recommend focused exercises built around speed and active word recall, such as timed category drills, flashcard recall, and rapid reading summaries. (iStock)
Instead of using generic puzzle apps, Voskuhl recommends paying attention to where you stumble in daily life and picking games that match those challenges.

People "know themselves," she said — "what they are bad at or what they used to be good at and now they’re not as good at ... Once you know those things, you should think about what kind of games [to play]. You can play around with different games. You can see if it pushes you."

title: Selena Gomez's vaping admission highlights hidden health risks doctors say millions face daily
summary: Selena Gomez called vaping "stupid" after it altered her voice, but doctors warn the health risks go beyond vocal cord damage for millions.
story: High-potency nicotine, constant puffing and difficult withdrawal can make vaping hard to quit. Addiction experts explain why some users return to cigarettes—and how treating dependence may help break the cycle.

When Selena Gomez revealed to her millions of followers that heavy nicotine vaping had noticeably altered her voice, calling the habit "stupid," her confession highlighted a larger issue with the practice.

For the singer and actress, the physical toll manifested in her vocal cords. But medical professionals emphasize that her experience is only a visible symptom of a deeper health crisis affecting millions of Americans who use e-cigarettes every day.

While often marketed as a safer alternative to conventional cigarettes, e-cigarettes pose significant health risks. Aside from the immediate vocal strain and airway inflammation noted by otolaryngologists, major health institutions warn that regular vaping exposes the body to a cocktail of toxic chemicals, cardiovascular strain and respiratory risks.
SELENA GOMEZ WARNS FANS AFTER VAPING HABIT LEAVES HER WITH PERMANENT CONSEQUENCE
Specialists emphasize that e-cigarettes deliver more concentrated doses of nicotine than traditional cigarettes, rapidly driving chemical dependency in the brain.

"With e-cigarettes and vaping, you can get a very high dose of nicotine, and that directly correlates to addiction and how difficult it can be to break these patterns," Trent Carter, a nurse practitioner and CEO of Renew Health in New Mexico, previously told Fox News Digital.
Selena Gomez’s public admission about vaping altering her voice underscores that vocal strain is merely one sign of broader health damage. (Getty Images)
Carter notes that high nicotine intake without traditional smoke can carry its own health consequences.

"It can lead to sleep disturbances, increased anxiety, and if you have underlying cardiac problems or high blood pressure, it’s going to raise your heart rate and elevate your blood pressure, leading to all sorts of issues."

According to the American Lung Association, the aerosol produced by e-cigarettes contains fine chemical particles, heavy metals such as nickel and lead, and organic compounds. Over time, inhaling these irritants can trigger chronic airway inflammation, irreversible lung tissue scarring, and obstructive pulmonary conditions.
NEVER SMOKED A CIGARETTE? YOU COULD STILL BE AT HIGHER RISK FOR LUNG CANCER
A major concern among physicians is the chemical composition of e-liquids. Even nicotine-free formulas contain flavorings and solvent agents like propylene glycol and vegetable glycerin.
When heated by the device’s coil, these liquids break down into toxic compounds, including formaldehyde and acrolein, both known to damage cellular structures in the respiratory system.
The continuous, all-day accessibility of vape devices creates a seamless behavioral routine that can lead to hundreds of puffs daily. (iStock)

Doctors stress that because modern e-cigarettes have only been widely used for a little over a decade, long-term health consequences are still unclear. While immediate effects may appear as hoarseness, coughing, or reduced athletic endurance, the larger impact poses risks to long-term vital organ function.
For many attempting to quit vaping, traditional tools like nicotine patches or gum can fall short because they don't address the psychological habit.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"While a patch or gum can help with physical cravings, if you aren't addressing the behavioral aspect, you're missing a huge component," Carter said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Beyond physical cravings, high-dose nicotine consumption elevates heart rate and blood pressure while exacerbating issues like anxiety and sleep disruption. (iStock)
"Vaping can become constant throughout the day. Subconsciously, you might not even realize how frequently you're doing it, or that you're using it to cope with underlying anxiety or lack of sleep."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
For those inspired by Gomez, health professionals urge people to seek comprehensive support rather than simply switch nicotine delivery methods.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"The goal shouldn't be to find another way to consume nicotine, it should be to treat the dependence itself," said Carter.

title: Catholic drinking habits are changing as Americans rethink alcohol's risks
summary: Catholic adults now report drinking rates near the levels of Protestants as shifting health views and social habits reshape moderate drinking in America.
story: Josh Gowin explains how research has shifted the understanding of alcohol's health risks, including its association with reduced brain volume, as drinking habits and social norms continue to change.

A historic shift in American drinking habits shows Catholic alcohol consumption reaching record lows, though scientific experts caution against attributing the drop strictly to religious or cultural changes.
The share of Catholic adults in the United States who report drinking alcohol has fallen to 55%, according to a Gallup report authored by analyst Frank Newport.
That marks a decline from the 2002–2004 period, when 79% of Catholics reported consuming alcoholic beverages. Over that same timeframe, self-reported Protestant drinking rates remained flat at 54%.
HEAVY DRINKING SURGES AMONG AMERICANS IN ONE AGE GROUP AS OTHER GENERATIONS CUT BACK
"Drinking has dropped significantly within both the group of those who have no religious identity and, in particular, among Catholics," Newport wrote in the analysis.
However, experts urged caution when drawing sweeping conclusions from subgroup survey data.

Dr. Joshua Gowin, an associate professor in the Department of Radiology at the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus who studies alcohol's effects on the brain, noted that self-reported polling figures can fluctuate based on sampling.
Historically, Catholics were far more likely to drink than Protestants, but a sharp drop in Catholic drinking has completely eliminated that long-standing gap. (iStock)
"There's definitely a general pattern of alcohol use decreasing across groups," Gowin told Fox News Digital.
"As far as the subgroups go, it wasn't clear or necessarily compelling to me that one group was showing a broad trend that wasn't reflected in the other groups," he went on.
BRAD PITT SAYS HE CAN DRINK IN ‘RESTRAINED MANNER’ AFTER 7 SOBER YEARS, BUT EXPERT RAISES RED FLAG
"It seemed like really only one data point showed that effect ... which made me a little skeptical that this is a broader phenomenon versus a single survey sample."
Despite methodological limitations in tracking specific religious subgroups, researchers agree that broader social and health trends are driving a shift in overall drinking habits.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Gallup findings indicate that a majority of Americans now view moderate drinking — defined as one or two drinks per day — as bad for their health.
In the latest polling, 52% of Catholics said moderate alcohol consumption is bad for health, alongside 56% of adults with no religious affiliation and 48% of Protestants.
Perceptions surrounding alcohol health risks have changed, with a majority across all religious demographics now viewing moderate drinking (one to two drinks daily) as bad for their health. (iStock)
Gowin noted that this public shift reflects decades of neuroscience and medical research.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"Twenty years ago, there was still kind of a push and pull between some benefits of alcohol and then some things that even then we knew were potentially harmful," he said.
"It's not like the serious problems have gone away."
"Over time, we've gotten a lot more clarity on the things that are bad for our health ... the balance has just shifted more in favor of the evidence for negative health effects."
Gowin pointed out that large-scale neuroimaging studies now consistently link higher alcohol consumption to reduced brain volume, reinforcing public health warnings.
The report’s author cautioned that the drop may reflect normal survey variation rather than a long-term cultural shift. (iStock)
Researchers also attribute shifting consumption patterns to broader societal changes, including shifts in social behavior and loneliness.
Much of America's alcohol consumption has historically occurred in group settings, and changes in how people gather socially may be influencing drinking habits, they believe.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
At the same time, experts caution that a drop in general social drinking does not mean severe alcohol problems have dissolved.

"One of the things that is a bit of a contradiction ... is that although the overall prevalence among all adults is down for the number of drinkers, there is actually a larger number of alcohol-related deaths in the past few years," Gowin noted.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"It's not like the serious problems have gone away."

title: Jalen Hurts puts spotlight on blood thinners: 5 mistakes that could put patients at risk
summary: Jalen Hurts' blood clot diagnosis puts blood thinners in the spotlight. Experts reveal five critical mistakes patients on anticoagulants must avoid.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel joins 'America's Newsroom' to break down Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts' diagnosis of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary emboli.
Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts' diagnosis of blood clots in both lungs has put blood thinners in the spotlight.
Hurts is receiving treatment with the medication and is expected to miss the remainder of the 2026 season, according to the NFL.
Even young, physically active people can develop dangerous blood clots, especially when risk factors such as an injury, long travel or recent surgery combine.
"Being in shape lowers your risk, but it doesn’t make you immune," said Dr. Joseph V. Lombardi, chief physician executive at AtlantiCare.
CHRISTINA APPLEGATE'S MS MISDIAGNOSIS AFTER 5 YEARS OF TREATMENT EXPOSES ALARMING MEDICAL REALITY
Hurts’ case also highlights the precautions patients taking blood thinners may need to follow.
Jalen Hurts is taking blood thinners to treat blood clots in his lungs, a treatment that can raise the risk of serious bleeding after an injury. (Mitchell Leff/Getty Images)

The medication can help prevent dangerous clots from growing or forming but can also make it harder for the body to stop bleeding after an injury, a concern for athletes playing high-contact sports or anyone who falls or gets hurt.

"Taking [blood thinners] consistently, understanding potential interactions and recognizing warning signs can greatly reduce the risk of complications," Dr. Yazan Abou-Ismail, a hematologist and thrombosis expert at the University of Utah, told Fox News Digital.
STACKING SUPPLEMENTS WITHOUT KEY TEST CAN DO MORE HARM THAN GOOD, EXPERT WARNS
Here are five mistakes patients should avoid:
Patients taking blood thinners should check with a doctor or pharmacist before adding new medications or supplements, experts say. (iStock)
1. Stopping treatment without medical guidance

While some patients only need blood thinners for a limited time, others may need them long term. When a clot has a clear cause, such as an injury, treatment often lasts about three months, Lombardi told Fox News Digital.

The duration depends on factors including the reason for treatment and whether a patient has had previous clots, Abou-Ismail added. Stopping too soon can raise the risk of another clot, while continuing longer than prescribed may increase bleeding risk.
SILENT INFLAMMATION COULD BE DAMAGING YOUR BODY — AND 5 HABITS MAY HELP KEEP IT IN CHECK
Patients should not stop or extend treatment without speaking with a doctor.
2. Skipping or doubling doses
Treatment with blood thinners varies, so patients should ask a healthcare team about doses, side effects and safe activities. (Getty Images)
Missing doses repeatedly can weaken a medication's protection against clots, Abou-Ismail said, but what to do after a missed dose depends on the specific drug.
Patients should follow the instructions for the prescription or call a pharmacist or doctor, not automatically take an extra dose to make up for a missed one.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
3. Adding medications or supplements without checking

Aspirin and NSAIDs, including ibuprofen, can increase bleeding risk when taken with blood thinners, Abou-Ismail said. Some prescription drugs and supplements, including fish oil and turmeric, can also affect bleeding or medication levels.
Patients should ask a doctor or pharmacist before taking anything new even if it is sold over the counter.
4. Brushing off signs of serious bleeding
Blood thinners can help prevent clots from growing, but they may also make bleeding harder to stop, doctors say. (Jeffrey Sauger/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Some bruising or minor bleeding may occur, but persistent nosebleeds, blood in the urine or unexplained increases in bruising warrant a call to a health care provider, Abou-Ismail said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Uncontrolled bleeding, vomiting blood, black or tarry stools, a sudden severe headache or new confusion, vision changes or trouble speaking require urgent care.
After a significant head injury, patients should seek medical evaluation, even if they initially feel fine, experts note.
5. Taking part in high-risk activities
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
A hard hit or fall can lead to serious bleeding in patients taking a blood thinner, which is why Hurts cannot play football during treatment.
Patients taking blood thinners may be able to continue exercising, but doctors advise avoiding contact sports and checking with their care team about activity risks. (iStock)
Patients should ask a doctor which activities are safe for them. Some may be able to continue exercising, but contact sports and other activities with a high risk of injury warrant extra caution.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Blood thinners do not dissolve an existing clot, Lombardi cautioned. They help prevent it from growing while the body clears it over time. The right treatment and precautions vary, so patients should contact their care team with questions about doses, side effects or activity.
Deirdre Bardolf is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital.

title: Christina Applegate's MS misdiagnosis after 5 years of treatment exposes alarming medical reality
summary: Christina Applegate's MS misdiagnosis highlights how brain lesions and common symptoms can mislead doctors, with nearly one in five referrals wrong.
story: Richard Ransohoff, M.D., a Boston-based neurologist who sits on the Board of Directors for the American Brain Foundation, spoke with Fox News Digital about why multiple sclerosis misdiagnoses are common.

Christina Applegate’s recent revelation that she was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis is raising questions about how the disease can be confused with other conditions even after years of treatment.
The actress, 54, shared the news during an Oct. 20 episode of her podcast, "MeSsy," alongside co-host Jamie-Lynn Sigler, saying she was in a complete "state of shock."

Applegate was first diagnosed with MS in 2021 after experiencing debilitating symptoms and undergoing extensive testing, including brain and spinal MRIs and a spinal tap. She said doctors found dozens of lesions on her brain.
CHRISTINA APPLEGATE SAYS SHE WAS MISDIAGNOSED WITH MS AND IS NOW 'BACK AT SQUARE ONE'
After years of treatment, her doctor decided to stop her regular infusions and monitor her B cells.

"And my B cells didn't change. They didn't go higher. They didn't go lower. They didn't change, and she had never seen that. So, I guess that began kind of a study into my diagnosis," Applegate shared.
Christina Applegate’s recent revelation that she was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis is raising questions about how the disease can be confused with other conditions. (AFP via Getty Images)
After additional brain scans, the doctor entered Applegate’s room and said, "Congratulations, you don't have MS."
The actress did not consider this to be good news, however.
"Because you don't get misdiagnosed and then all of a sudden [you’re] better," she said. "I haven't gotten better. … If anything, I've gotten worse in some ways."
CARLY SIMON REVEALS THE COMMON CONDITION THAT MASKED HER PARKINSON'S DIAGNOSIS
Applegate noted that she has "every symptom" of someone with MS, adding that there are many conditions that mirror the disease.
"There is no single element in the diagnostic process that tells you with 100% certainty that it is MS."

She recalled that her MRIs clearly showed around 30 lesions but said her neurologist identified a different feature, which she described as a "string," that led to the conclusion that she did not have MS.
"So, I'm back at square one [and] don't know what's going on with me."
Why MS can be misdiagnosed
Dr. Marwa Kaisey, an associate professor of neurology at Cedars-Sinai in Los Angeles, said during a follow-up "MeSsy" podcast episode that misdiagnosis of MS is "fairly common."

In a study of patients referred to MS clinics at UCLA and Cedars-Sinai, Kaisey, who has not treated Applegate, said she found that nearly one in five who arrived with an MS diagnosis ultimately did not have the disease.
BRAIN TUMOR FOUND DURING PREVENTIVE SCAN PUTS FULL-BODY MRIS BACK IN THE SPOTLIGHT
"Some [had been diagnosed] for decades," she said. "And a majority of them were on medication to treat their MS."
The primary challenge, according to the doctor, is that there is no single test for MS.
"It's not like we have something like a pregnancy test that says, yes, you have it, no, you don't," Kaisey said.
Instead, Kaisey said, "It's a list of criteria, some of which remain a little bit subjective."
New clues on brain scans
Most misdiagnosed patients did have some type of white matter spots, or lesions, on their MRI scans, Kaisey noted, but they had a different cause that was not MS.
Newer imaging techniques may help doctors distinguish MS lesions from white matter spots caused by other conditions.
Most misdiagnosed patients did have some type of white matter spots, or lesions, on their MRI scans, Kaisey noted, but they had a different cause that was not MS. (iStock)

Kaisey pointed to the "central vein sign," an MRI finding that looks for small blood vessels running through the center of lesions, which is a characteristic associated with MS. The sign was incorporated into updated MS diagnostic criteria to help doctors determine whether white matter lesions are consistent with the disease.

Richard Ransohoff, M.D., a Boston-based neurologist who sits on the Board of Directors for the American Brain Foundation, called the central vein sign "a real step forward" in distinguishing MS lesions from other abnormalities.
"Things are getting better, and even in the time that Ms. Applegate has been having her symptoms and her evaluation, things have gotten better," said Ransohoff, who also has not treated the actress.
SELMA BLAIR'S LAWYER CITES MISSED MEDICATION, HEAD INJURY AFTER IN-FLIGHT ARREST: WHAT DOCTORS SAY
Many of the symptoms of MS, such as tingling or numbness in the feet, fatigue and brain fog, are common in other conditions, according to both neurologists.

"To distinguish MS from its mimics can be challenging, and doctors, even with the best intentions … can sometimes still get it wrong," Kaisey said. "To diagnose MS, we need a symptom that's kind of very specific to MS, and we also need the MRI that looks like MS."
Despite the potential for diagnostic uncertainty, doctors emphasized that the outlook for people who do have MS has improved dramatically. (iStock)

Kaisey said she has found that being "undiagnosed" with MS can be even harder than receiving the initial diagnosis, particularly when the disease has become intertwined with someone's identity, family and community.
"So, to suddenly take that away, I think it’s earth-shattering. It's life-changing in a huge way."
EARLY PARKINSON’S SYMPTOMS MISDIAGNOSED FOR YEARS, TERRY CREWS’ WIFE REVEALS
The neurologist emphasized that patients should feel comfortable asking questions and getting a second opinion.
"Don't be afraid to do that, especially if something inside is telling you that you need to dig a little deeper," she advised.
MS-mimicking conditions
Ransohoff reiterated that MS misdiagnoses are common.
"It’s a tough diagnosis, and there is no single element in the diagnostic process that tells you with 100% certainty that it is MS," he told Fox News Digital.
The neurologist said even after a diagnosis, doctors should "keep an open mind" and be willing to reconsider.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"If things start going differently from your expectations, if the person begins to have symptoms that really don't fit in with MS or they don't respond to treatment, then you really start to put on your thinking cap and say, ‘What else could this be?’
"It requires the ultimate in humility as a physician. You simply have to say there are certain things we know and certain things we don't know."
Christina Applegate attends the 28th Annual Critics Choice Awards at Fairmont Century Plaza Jan. 15, 2023, in Los Angeles. (Getty Images for Critics Choice Association)
Classic early MS symptoms tend to appear relatively quickly, persist for weeks and then recede, according to Ransohoff.

Anything producing a similar pattern can potentially mimic the disease. Some of those conditions may include certain strokes in younger people, neuromyelitis optica spectrum disease (a rare autoimmune disease of the central nervous system), MOG antibody disease (a rare autoimmune inflammatory disorder), lupus and migraine, he said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
A migraine is one of the most common alternative diagnoses, both neurologists agreed.
Kaisey noted a migraine can also produce MRI abnormalities in the form of white spots, although they are usually smaller and in a different shape and location.
"Facing the unknown when you feel crappy is a very tough road to go."
"If you're not looking closely at the MRI or you don't know exactly what to look for, you can confuse the two," she said.
In some cases, reversing an MS diagnosis can actually provide a concrete alternative diagnosis and better targeted treatment, but that did not happen in Applegate’s case, Ransohoff noted.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"You have to have tremendous sympathy for her suffering in that context, because even when treatment is not going as well as you would like, it's better to know what you're dealing with," he said.
"Facing the unknown when you feel crappy is a very tough road to go."
Specialized care

To prevent misdiagnosis, Ransohoff recommends that everyone who receives a multiple sclerosis diagnosis is seen by a specialist at a specialty MS center who has developed pattern recognition after many occurrences of seeing the disease.
The neurologist noted that MS treatment has advanced dramatically over the course of his career, growing from virtually no options to more than 20 medications today.
Neurologists recommend that everyone who receives a multiple sclerosis diagnosis is seen by a specialist at a specialty MS center. (iStock)
"You want to work with someone who has experience with all those medicines, with all the various patterns that MS can show, because every person's MS is different," he said.
If a treatment isn’t helping or is causing significant side effects, an MS specialist can reassess the approach and help identify a more appropriate medication, Ransohoff added.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The doctor emphasized that the outlook for people who do have MS has improved dramatically.

"The person who's diagnosed with MS today is totally different from 40 years ago when I got started," the neurologist said. "If the diagnosis is correct and the treatment is correct, then they should do pretty well with their MS."
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Knee treatment without surgery offers lasting pain relief for 80% of arthritis patients, study finds
summary: A non-surgical knee osteoarthritis treatment uses dissolvable gelatin particles to block excess blood vessels, reducing inflammation without implants, researchers say.
story: A non-surgical knee procedure provided yearlong pain relief for 80% of patients in a new study. The treatment reduces inflammation without permanent implants, but researchers note important limitations.
A non-surgical procedure that temporarily blocks extra blood vessels in the knee is offering lasting pain relief for people with knee osteoarthritis.
In a clinical study of 194 patients, 80% of them reported significant reductions in knee pain that lasted for at least a full year after receiving the treatment.
The findings highlight a potential alternative for millions of adults with chronic joint pain who have outgrown pain medications or steroid injections — but who want to avoid total knee replacement.
WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY FIGHT 7 SERIOUS HEALTH PROBLEMS BEFORE THE POUNDS EVEN COME OFF
Osteoarthritis wears down joint cartilage and causes the body to grow unnecessary new blood vessels around the knee, according to Mayo Clinic.
These extra vessels increase inflammation and irritate surrounding nerves, making daily movement painful.
Up to 80% of knee osteoarthritis patients in a new study experienced clinically meaningful, long-term pain reduction lasting at least one full year. (iStock)
The procedure, known as genicular artery embolization (GAE), addresses this directly.
By temporarily clogging excess blood vessels, doctors can reduce inflammation and quiet pain-sensing nerves without major surgery or permanent implants.

Because the treatment uses microscopic gelatin particles that dissolve over time, it leaves no foreign material behind. If widely adopted, GAE could provide a repeatable, low-risk way for patients to stay active and preserve joint function longer, researchers say.
"We saw a significant drop in pain and a significant increase in function."

"For many patients with knee osteoarthritis, there is a real treatment gap today," said Florian Nima Fleckenstein, M.D., deputy head of Interventional Radiology Campus Mitte, Charité-Universitätsmedizin Berlin, in a press release.

"Our study demonstrates that GAE using rapidly resorbable gelatin-based microspheres is a safe, minimally invasive therapy that provides meaningful pain relief and functional improvement in participants with osteoarthritis-related knee symptoms for at least 12 months."
ALZHEIMER’S RISK LINKED TO COMPOUND FOUND IN POPULAR JOINT HEALTH SUPPLEMENTS
During GAE, doctors use real-time X-ray guidance to steer a thin, flexible tube into the blood vessels surrounding the knee joint.
Then they release tiny, dissolvable gelatin particles into specific vessels to slow excess blood flow to the inflamed areas.
Unlike traditional joint implants, the microscopic gelatin particles dissolve naturally over time after calming local inflammation. (iStock)
Across 239 total procedures performed on 194 study participants, none experienced severe complications.
Only 6.7% reported mild side effects, such as brief skin discoloration or minor bruising, issues that resolved on their own.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"In our cohort, we saw a significant drop in pain and a significant increase in function, including sports and recreation and daily activity," Fleckenstein said.
"Most importantly, their quality of life significantly increased."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

In addition to feeling less pain, participants experienced gains in daily mobility. Patients reported easier walking, climbing stairs and bending, while overall quality-of-life scores more than doubled over the 12-month follow-up period.
Limitations of study
While the results are promising, researchers note several important limitations.
First, the study did not include a control group receiving a mock or placebo procedure.

Because the study on knee pain lacked a placebo control group and tracked outcomes for only 12 months, larger randomized trials are needed to confirm the long-term duration and physiological impact of the new treatment. (iStock)
Without a comparison group, it is difficult to isolate the physical benefits of the dissolvable particles from potential placebo effects, the researchers said.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Second, the study tracked patients for only one year.
Further research is needed to determine how long the pain relief typically lasts and how often repeat treatments might be required.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Finally, while GAE effectively reduces inflammation and pain, the researchers said it is not a cure.
The procedure does not rebuild lost cartilage or reverse structural joint damage. Larger, randomized trials are currently underway to confirm these early findings.
Fox News Digital reached out to the study authors for further comment.
