Yelich, 34, and 33-year-old reliever Brandon Woodruff, whose save in Game 3 was his first appearance since July 4 because of injuries, were the only players remaining from a 2018 Brewers roster that was just one win away from that season’s World Series.

In the divisional round against San Diego, 20-year-old outfielder Jackson Chourio hit a late two-run homer that saved Milwaukee in its opening game of the postseason. Chourio then delivered a walk-off single to win the following game.

On the mound, Milwaukee constructed a feared rotation of arms starting with Misiorowski, the 24-year-old with blazing speed who made the All-Star Game as a rookie in 2025 after just five starts. For his encore, Misiorowski in 2026 led a pitching staff that allowed MLB’s second-lowest team ERA during the regular season. When he left games, a bullpen with arms just as nasty and hard-throwing as Misiorowski’s took over.
“This is just incredible,” Megill, on the mound for the final out, said after the win. “Ten-year-old me would be so proud.”
All of the pieces worked, all season. When the regular season ended, Milwaukee stood alone at the top of the standings.
And when the playoffs ended a month later, the Brewers were on top yet again. Their long wait for a title had ended.

title: Manhunt grows for escaped murderer who may have left area where truck was ditched
summary: Jacob Morley, who fatally shot a co-worker, escaped Sunday from a prison in Tennessee. The work truck he allegedly stole was found in Illinois.
story: Jacob Morley, a convicted killer on the loose since Sunday, has no known connection to the small Illinois town where the truck he is accused of stealing was found, the police chief said Wednesday.
“What we have seen kind of leads us in the direction that he’s not still here. But that doesn’t mean that we’ve stopped looking,” Marion Police Chief David Fitts said.

Morley, 28, convicted of killing a co-worker in 2022, was serving a life sentence when he escaped from Northwest Correctional Complex in Tiptonville, Tennessee, sometime before 11:30 p.m. Sunday, officials there said.

Morley had stolen a work truck, and early Tuesday that truck was found behind a business in Marion, a town of around 16,000 that is around 100 miles north of Tiptonville, authorities in Marion and Tennessee said.
There have been no reports in Marion of any other stolen vehicles, and there was no evidence around the truck that was found, Fitts said.
There have also been no confirmed sightings, he said.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
“There’s really nowhere for him to go here where he wouldn’t be recognized. His face is all over the news,” Fitts said.
Morley has no known connection to Marion or southern Illinois, he said.

“Have no idea why he would come here, other than I-57 is a major interstate and it runs right through the middle of our town,” Fitts said. “And I don’t know, maybe he was low on gas and just pulled off. I don’t know.”
Morley was convicted of first-degree murder, abuse of a corpse, tampering with evidence and aggravated burglary after a trial in February 2025. He also pleaded guilty to theft of property.
He was accused of shooting Cody Birchfield in the back of the head in 2022, according to court documents. Birchfield’s body was found in a large metal box under Morley’s residence, the documents say.
Birchfield’s sister, Carrie Norman, said Wednesday that “it feels like a scary movie.”
The family, she said, “have to go back through the experience — once again. Once again, because you don’t know where he’s at, but you know what he’s capable of.”

Also Wednesday, the reward for information leading to Morley’s arrest increased from $2,500 to $15,000, a combined sum from the Tennessee governor’s office, the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation and the U.S. Marshals Service, the bureau said.
Fitts said he wished Morley had been caught, but he urged people not to take things into their own hands.

“This is really frustrating that we can’t find him. Somebody will eventually, I have no doubt in my mind. I wish it was us so we could catch him now,” Fitts said. “But, and I just want to let our people know that, again, don’t approach him. Call 911. We’ll handle it.”
Around 11:30 p.m. Sunday, prison staff members confirmed that Morley was unaccounted for and conducted an emergency count and search of the facility, the Tennessee Department of Correction said.
Security video showed Morley “breached the perimeter fence and exited the facility in his TDOC uniform,” the department said.
The department has not given more details about how the escape occurred, which it said Wednesday is under investigation.

title: California judge denies Trump DOJ request to segregate alleged noncitizen ballots
summary: A federal judge in California on Wednesday refused the Trump administration’s request to segregate 20,000 mail-in ballots from individuals it alleges are noncitizens.
story: A federal judge in California on Wednesday refused the Trump administration’s request to segregate 20,000 mail-in ballots from individuals it alleges are noncitizens.

“This request violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections,” U.S. District Judge David Carter wrote. “If Plaintiff’s last-minute request for relief were granted, either party could create chaos for their own political purposes to disrupt the election process.”

What the administration was asking for, he wrote, “would wreak havoc and disrupt the election that is already underway, create a chilling effect on election workers and voters alike, and discount the votes of United States citizens.”
He also questioned whether the government’s claims of over 20,000 noncitizen voters were accurate.

“Given the vagueness of Plaintiff’s descriptions of its procedures and the unreliability of its similar claims in other states, the Court cannot conclude that Plaintiff’s process is credible,” Carter wrote, pointing to similar allegations the administration had made in a neighboring state.

“In Nevada, DHS initially identified up to 15,903 registered voters as noncitizens based on ‘high-confidence’ matches, but later reduced that number to 6,218, and then to 185 after conducting its manual review. Nevada officials later confirmed that all 185 individuals were citizens,” the judge wrote.

“Had Nevada officials accepted Plaintiff’s allegations there as true, 185 citizens would have been deprived of their vote. This Court will not deprive Californians who have met the requirements for voter registration of their fundamental right because of Plaintiff’s unfounded allegations.”

The Justice Department filed the suit Oct. 15, seeking a court order that the state “set aside vote-by-mail ballots from persons identified by the Federal Government likely to be noncitizens” and not count them until their citizenship is confirmed.
The department said it had compiled “a list of over 20,000 names of people” the government “believes are likely non-citizens.”

Attorneys for the state countered that the government’s numbers are unreliable. In a July letter, it put the number of suspect voters at 190,000 and has refused to release information about how it has generated its lists.
“Where is the evidence?” an attorney representing California, Christina McCall, said at the hearing Tuesday, calling the government’s allegations “vague” and “not reliable.”

Another attorney for the state, Anne Bellows, told the judge “the stakes here are enormous,” arguing the government was trying to force California to initiate an unclear investigation into the citizenship of tens of thousands of people without any clear standards shortly before an election.
It “is a recipe for disenfranchisement,” Bellows said.
First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli told Carter: “We’re not telling California what they have to do. We’re telling them what they can’t do.”
Essayli said that once the state is made aware of potential noncitizens on its voter rolls, “they need to do something.”
“What they cannot do is do nothing and proceed to count the votes,” he said.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
The judge said that if the government believes there is noncitizen voting, which is a crime, it should bring charges.

“Don’t you have the power of indictments?” Carter asked Essayli. “You brought 28 indictments,” he said, referring to a recent announcement by prosecutors of people who have been found to have voted illegally in California in recent years. “You may find others. You have the right to bring that indictment against them.”
“You’ve got a remedy, for goodness’ sakes,” Carter said. “Go out and indict.”
Essayli on Wednesday bashed the judge’s ruling and said an appeal is underway.

“Every day, more ballots are processed by election officials. This ongoing emergency disenfranchises American citizens through dilution,” he said in a statement. “The Solicitor General authorized an immediate appeal. We filed our Notice of Appeal and will immediately seek an emergency order from the Ninth Circuit.”

The Justice Department has already been to a federal appeals court once in the case. It filed a motion to expedite the case to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals last week, after Carter did not act on its request to rule in the matter by Thursday.
The appeals court held an emergency hearing Sunday and ruled against the administration 2-1 on Monday.
The majority found it did not have jurisdiction because Carter had not yet ruled, but it found the government’s “claimed emergency” was at least partly “a self-constructed one.”
“At least part of the delay here is attributable to the United States’s own delay in filing suit,” Circuit Judge Mark Bennett wrote in the ruling.

“The United States has taken issue with California’s voter rolls since at least July 16, when it sent a letter to California’s secretary of state citing its ‘[p]reliminary’ analysis of California’s voter rolls. And neither California’s law permitting the processing of ballots twenty-nine days before an election, nor its law providing for the issuance of mail-in ballots to registered voters, is new,” he wrote.

Circuit Judge Gabriel Sanchez wrote in a concurring opinion that the government was asking the “court to dictate to a state legislature a matter squarely within the state’s traditional domain, upending the state’s policies in this regard and inviting disorder and confusion for voters and election officials alike.”

The dissenting judge, Trump appointee Patrick Bumatay, wrote, “We should’ve granted the federal government relief — federal law precludes California from commingling ballots likely cast by aliens with legitimate ballots, because it encourages and induces illegal voting.”

title: Hayden Panettiere’s death is ruled accidental and police investigation is closed
summary: Panettiere, 36, died of the toxic effects of multiple drugs, including fentanyl, the coroner determined.
story: Actor Hayden Panettiere’s death has been ruled an accident and the case is now closed, police in South Carolina announced Wednesday.

“Based on the Medical Examiner’s determination and the findings of the investigation, Hayden Panettiere’s death has been ruled accidental,” Greenville police said, noting the investigation has concluded.
Panettiere, 36, the actor who starred in the shows “Heroes” and “Nashville,” was found unresponsive on Aug. 16 in a South Carolina apartment complex where she was staying.
Last month, the Greenville County Coroner’s Office ruled her death an accident caused by the toxic effects of multiple drugs: fentanyl, 4-ANPP, alprazolam, methocarbamol and quetiapine.
The coroner said there were no signs of trauma that would have contributed to her death. Police also have said no signs of foul play were found during the initial response and investigation.
Panettiere, who had publicly discussed her struggle with addiction, had been in rehab just weeks before, according to the coroner’s report.

Panettiere’s on-again, off-again boyfriend, Brian Hickerson, was at the apartment complex at the time of her death. He showed police a “bag of medication” he said she was taking at the time, according to the police report.

After the coroner’s report was issued, Panettiere’s mother, Lesley Vogel, called her daughter a “fighter” who was “transparent with her addictions and her numerous rehab attempts show her resolve to live a healthy life.”
Vogel also said at the time that she had “never heard Hayden speak of fentanyl.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

The Drug Enforcement Administration was also investigating, a source familiar with the probe previously told NBC News. The agency typically looks into the narcotics involved in a case, how they were obtained and whether any laws were broken in procuring the drugs.
Panettiere entered Hollywood as a child actor and later carved her own path, starring in the films “Remember the Titans,” “Ice Princess” and “Bring It On: All or Nothing.”

In her memoir, “This Is Me: A Reckoning,” she detailed how her life began to spiral after she had a daughter with Ukrainian heavyweight boxing champion Wladimir Klitschko in 2014. She began drinking heavily to cope with postpartum depression and Klitschko’s distance, she wrote in the book.
She checked into rehab and gave Klitschko custody of their child in 2018.
In the book, she also discussed grappling with pain and grief after her brother, Jansen Panettiere, died in 2023 from an undiagnosed heart condition.

If you or someone you know is struggling with a drug or substance abuse problem, call these numbers for help: The Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration’s national helpline is 1-800-662-HELP (1-800-662-4357); the National Drug Helpline is 1-844-289-0879; and the American Addiction Centers’ hotline is (866) 464-3073.

title: Meet the Democrats trying to flip the script on gun rights: From the Politics Desk
summary: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
story: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.

In today’s edition, Frank Thorp V and Ryan Nobles speak with Democratic candidates who are touting their gun credentials. Plus, Andrea Mitchell digs into President Donald Trump’s potential next moves on Iran.
— Adam Wollner
Meet the Democrats trying to flip the script on gun rights
A group of Democratic candidates on the ballot next week are hoping to start a new conversation around guns as part of a strategy to win back rural voters in red-leaning areas.

Wisconsin’s 1st District: Democrat Mitchell Berman’s ads have portrayed him as a proud gun owner and hunter. One shows him fishing while wearing a handgun in a holster; another shows him skeet shooting with clay pigeons labeled “Data Centers.” After the target explodes in the air, his 6-year-old daughter yells, “Great shot, Dad!”

“That’s who I am,” Berman told NBC News. “When I go fishing up north — where I’m from we have wolves. We have — in spring trout season, we have bears that are coming out of their dens with cubs. We’ve even had a mountain lion on our trail camera. So, you know, when I go out into the woods, I carry a sidearm with me for protection.”

His race against GOP Rep. Bryan Steil was not expected to be close. President Donald Trump carried the district in 2020 and 2024, and Steil won re-election two years ago by 10 points. But polling has shown the race is within reach for Democrats.

Texas’ 15th District: Bobby Pulido, a Tejano singer-turned-Democratic congressional candidate, is not shy about his love for guns and hunting. He’s posted videos of him shooting a target a mile away, and his rec room is lined with the trophies he’s gathered on hunts. He even named his oldest son Remington.
“Listen, in the rural areas, firearms are a way of life,” Pulido told NBC News, saying that fundraisers in the Rio Grande Valley are more common at skeet shooting events than at golf courses.

Pulido is also running in an area that Trump won in the last two presidential elections. The district was redrawn earlier this year to make it more favorable for Republicans, but a shift in the Latino vote away from Trump mixed with a struggling economy has put Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz at risk of losing her bid for re-election.
Read more →
The big decision awaiting Trump after the midterms

On the campaign trail, President Donald Trump has been confidently promising that oil prices will drop like a rock after the midterms — especially skyrocketing diesel fuel critical in farm states that could decide which party wins the Senate. Implicit is that he will attempt to do something decisive after next week to end the war against Iran and fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

His not-so-subtle hints are backed up by new reporting in The Wall Street Journal and other publications that the U.S. has told Gulf partners it will resume intense, brief strikes against Iran after the midterms. And Israel’s hawkish Trump ally Benjamin Netanyahu has at least temporarily retained a caretaker role as prime minister while he and his rival, former Army Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot, jockey for a majority. In Israel’s complex parliamentary system, a decisive outcome could take weeks or months, or even lead to another election.

That places Netanyahu in control of a potential resumption of the war, a position he had advocated for before Israelis went to the polls, according to The New York Times and other outlets. According to those reports, Israel’s military and intelligence leaders effectively vetoed that option, saying it would politicize their decision-making.
For Subscribers

As flawed as Israel’s democracy has been in many respects, according to many of its own citizens and even many longtime U.S. supporters, it still has the virtue of a largely independent military. But in the U.S., critics fear that may not be the case with the civilian leadership of the military in the second Trump administration.
For Subscribers

In past administrations in both political parties, secretaries of defense and their top deputies were usually experienced foreign policy or former military leaders, willing to offer independent opinions to the presidents they served in a formalized National Security Council interagency system. Conflicting options were debated in a deliberative process before they were presented to the commander in chief.

Yes, on occasion, chief executives were misled by false narratives, like those delivered during the Vietnam War by Defense Secretary Robert McNamara. Or, during the Iraq quagmire, when the chain of command was short-circuited by a powerful personality like President George W. Bush’s defense secretary, Donald Rumsfeld. Notably, Rumsfeld was forced out of his role the morning after Bush’s party got hammered in the 2006 midterms.
Now, whether his party wins or loses in next week’s midterms, Trump faces what could be the most consequential decision of his second term: whether to “finish the job” and resume attacking Iran.

Such a decision would fly in the faces of European leaders who counsel that renewed strikes would lead to higher oil prices and a potential economic downturn and not produce a more compliant regime in Tehran. At the same time, there is now a growing consensus in Riyadh and other Gulf capitals that they need to find some accommodation with Iran to get the regime to try to restrain its Houthi proxies, who threaten to become an existential threat to their economies.

The question for Trump is whether to follow the advice of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the former Fox News personality who has purged many of the Pentagon’s most experienced top generals and has privately advocated for resuming military action against Iran.

The hawks could be right that a weakened Iran could be felled by a decisive blow, though skeptics note that such a strategy has not yet proved successful. The U.S. and global economy — to say nothing of Trump’s legacy — may well depend on what he decides in the next few weeks.

title: Ex-fiancé in ‘The People’s Court’ disappearance charged with murder after phone data review
summary: Dale Smith Jr., of Orlando, Florida, was arrested this month and charged with the second-degree murder of Michelle Parker.
story: A fresh look at cellphone data and text messages led to the arrest of a Florida man accused of murdering his ex-fiancée within hours of taping an episode for “The People’s Court” in 2011, court documents unsealed Tuesday revealed.
Dale Smith Jr., a 55-year-old Orlando resident, was taken into custody Oct. 14 and charged with second-degree murder in the death of Michelle Parker, whose body has never been found, police said.
Smith was 40 and Parker 33 when she was last seen alive on Nov. 17, 2011, the day the episode was taped. The two shared custody of twins at the time.

That afternoon, at about 2 p.m., Parker and Smith appeared for a taping of “The People’s Court” to settle a dispute over a $5,000 engagement ring she allegedly threw off a balcony. The judge ruled “that both parties were responsible for the ring and ordered they split the $5,000.00 damage,” according to an arrest warrant affidavit.
Smith told investigators that, after the taping of the show, Parker dropped the children off at his home and left about 10 minutes later, police said.
But surveillance cameras appeared to show that “the victim’s Hummer was at the suspect’s residence for at least one hour,” according to the affidavit.

Surveillance cameras showed Parker arriving at Smith’s building at about 3:18 p.m., according to the affidavit. At about 4:18 p.m. “victim and suspect phones leaves suspect’s home,” the document said.

By 4:32 p.m., the “victim’s and suspect’s phones continue moving west,” the affidavit said, a route that conflicted with Parker’s plans. “The victim was to travel north to pick up her oldest son who was waiting for her,” it said.

Parker’s brother, Dustin Erickson, also texted her that afternoon asking where she was. Her phone replied, “Waterford,” according to the affidavit. “Waterford” is the common local name for the Waterford Lakes Town Center shopping mall, about 12 miles northeast of Smith’s home.

“The victim’s cell phone never travels east or north towards the Waterford Lakes shopping center,” the affidavit said. “According to Dustin Erickson, the victim had no reason to deceive Dustin as to her location.”

Smith has previously said he had no idea where Parker went after dropping off the children. He told investigators he thought she was “laying low” after the “People’s Court” episode aired, the affidavit said.
“He wanted the victim to come home safe for their kids. However, according to his phone records, he never called or messaged her ever again after November 17, 2011,” the document said.
Police said Smith has a history of domestic violence. Detectives interviewed Jill Van Mechelen, another of his ex-fiancées, whom he knew before he met Parker.

“According to Jill Van Mechelen, the suspect would manually choke (strangle) her during these episodes of domestic physical violence,” the affidavit said. “The suspect also made threats to kill Jill Van Mechelen and her father. Jill Van Mechelen reported that the suspect told her on multiple occasions that he would kill her and/or her father and make them disappear.”
Smith’s attorney declined comment Wednesday, citing a court gag order.

title: Chiefs coach defends signing kicker suspended after sexual misconduct allegations
summary: Justin Tucker, 37, hasn’t played in the NFL since 2024. Coach Andy Reid said the team did “our homework” before it added him.
story: Kansas City Chiefs head coach Andy Reid offered only a short explanation Wednesday when he was asked why the team was comfortable signing kicker Justin Tucker, who has not played in the NFL since 2024 after a string of sexual misconduct allegations.
“He’s done his suspension. Took care of his business there. I’ll leave it at that,” Reid said when he was asked what message signing Tucker sent to female fans.
Asked what level of involvement team ownership had in the signing, Reid said, “We try to do our homework best way we possibly can and talk to a lot of people and make sure things are OK.”

On Wednesday, the Chiefs signed Tucker, 37, to their practice squad. Kansas City was looking for competition at the kicking position because of the poor performance of starting kicker Harrison Butker, who has missed five of his 16 field-goal attempts this season.

Tucker last played for the Baltimore Ravens during the 2024 season. In January 2025, The Baltimore Banner reported accounts from six women who accused Tucker of nonconsensual sexual behavior during massage therapy sessions from 2012 to 2016, including that he exposed his genitals and brushed women with his exposed penis. The following month, 10 more massage therapists came forward with more accusations against Tucker.
He denied all allegations at the time, initially describing them as “unequivocally false.”

“I maintain I did not act inappropriately at any point before, during, or after a professional bodywork treatment session, nor have I ever been told I am unwelcome at any massage therapy provider. These claims are simply not true,” Tucker said in a statement in February 2025. “It devastates me to know that anyone I have worked with would not have felt respected and valued as a professional, but more importantly as a person, and to anyone who has felt otherwise, I am sorry.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

The NFL suspended Tucker for the first 10 weeks of the 2025 season following an investigation, but he remained unsigned for the entire season. He worked out with the Miami Dolphins earlier this year, according to NFL reporter Aaron Wilson.

Asked about his decision-making process when it comes to signing a player such as Tucker, Reid said: “I try to do homework on it, see exactly what’s taken place since. He served a suspension; there’s been time involved with it. That’s how I evaluate it.”
Asked the kind of homework he did on Tucker, Reid said, “I’m not going to get into all of that.”
More from Sports

Rays stun Brewers with a rally in 12th inning, force World Series Game 5 with 4-3 winEven with early Game 6 tipoff, Valkyries are confident fans will find a way to watchArsenal knocked out of League Cup by League Two side Fleetwood Town

Even with early Game 6 tipoff, Valkyries are confident fans will find a way to watch
Arsenal knocked out of League Cup by League Two side Fleetwood Town
Reporters also asked Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes about the signing Wednesday, and he expressed confidence in the team’s front office.

“We had a lot of people that we’ve added in and out,” Mahomes said, per ESPN. “I try not to get too high or too low on anything. I know [general manager Brett] Veach [and the front office] do a great job of bringing great players in. But for me, it was about the Denver Broncos and moving on and continuing to get better.”
Tucker is second all time in the NFL in field-goal kicking percentage. He struggled during his final season with the Ravens, however, converting a career-worst 73.3% of his field-goal attempts.

title: Fed plans to eliminate some rate-setting meetings, chairman says
summary: The Federal Reserve plans to eliminate some meetings devoted to setting interest rates in the next couple of years, Chairman Kevin Warsh said Wednesday.
story: The Federal Reserve plans to eliminate some meetings devoted to setting interest rates in the next couple of years, Chairman Kevin Warsh said Wednesday.

Starting next fall, the central bank will dedicate one of its eight annual meetings to considering broad-based questions about the economy, rather than to voting on interest rates, Warsh said. That number will increase to two in 2028.
The chairman made the announcement following the release of the central bank’s latest policy announcement, which left rates unchanged.
He said the rationale for doing so was to devote more time to thinking about longer-term issues by shifting attention away from the immediate interest rate environment.

“Getting policy right involves assessing near-term developments at timely, regular and information-rich intervals,” he said. “But it’s equally important we reserve time and space as an intellectually diverse group for strategic deliberations, for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons.”

Warsh’s announcement marks a major shake-up for the Federal Reserve’s long-standing policy calendar, which is closely watched by investors around the world. The Federal Open Market Committee has held eight scheduled meetings a year since 1981.

Warsh began seriously discussing a reduction in rate-setting meetings in July, according to the FOMC’s meeting minutes, arguing that a longer lag between rate-setting meetings would allow the committee to accumulate more data about the economy.
For Subscribers

Reducing the number of rate-setting meetings has long been debated over concerns about shortsightedness — but the switch was never enacted over fears that the Fed would become less nimble in reacting to sudden changes in the economy.
For Subscribers
The change would make the Fed unique among major central banks, including the Bank of England and Bank of Japan.
It marks another major change enacted by Warsh, who took the reins of the Fed in May after being nominated by President Donald Trump.

Warsh has dramatically shortened the FOMC’s post-meeting policy statement. He has also declined to issue what is known as “forward guidance,” which contains forecasts about future inflation and unemployment.

title: Federal Reserve leaves interest rates unchanged despite rising inflation
summary: The soaring costs of gas, diesel and crude oil are a major driver of higher prices across the U.S. economy.
story: The Federal Reserve voted Wednesday to keep interest rates unchanged, its final monetary policy decision before the midterm elections.
The decision to hold rates steady came despite inflation that jumped from a 3.4% annual rate in August to 3.7% in September.

Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh also announced that the central bank will reduce the number of meetings at which it votes on interest rates from eight to seven next year and by two in 2028. Warsh said that the seismic change to the schedule would help improve the “quality” of its decisions.

A major driver of that inflation is the soaring cost of gas, diesel and crude oil. These higher prices have hit consumers hard, and many economists say the spillover effect of rising gas prices has started to show up across the broader economy.
In its post-decision statement, the Fed acknowledged the problem that inflation is causing but said it needs more data before moving forward with a rate hike.

“Inflation remains elevated. The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee’s 2 percent goal,” it said.
The Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, the personal consumption expenditures price index, will not be released until Thursday; it is expected to touch 3.7%.

“This suggests that the Fed might not be done tightening and future hikes will depend on the incoming data,” economists at Morgan Stanley said. In central bank speak, “tightening” refers to raising rates.

“As we widen the frame to survey the broad economic and financial picture, real activity is clearly pointing in the right direction,” Warsh said in a post-meeting news conference. “That’s good news, but inflation is too high.”
“Energy and related prices have moved higher again in recent weeks, and our job is to ensure that relative price changes in some sectors do not broaden out across the economy,” he added.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Wednesday’s vote was not unanimous, unlike September’s 12-0 vote to hike rates, the first time since 2023 that the central bank had raised its benchmark rate.

Two officials, governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, dissented in favor of a rate hike. The dissent by Cook, whom President Donald Trump is attempting to fire, was her first ever.
An interest rate hike could have added slightly more pressure to already beleaguered consumers.
Voters have consistently told pollsters that rising prices, especially in the housing and energy sectors, are their primary concerns as they cast their ballots.
The most recent NBC News poll found Trump’s approval rating at 27% for his handling of the cost of living and 29% for his handling of the Iran war.

Two-thirds of Americans said the soaring gas prices triggered by Trump’s Iran war were either a “very serious” or “somewhat serious” problem. More than half of respondents said current economic conditions had caused them to change what kinds of groceries they buy.
Warsh said the midterms and politics “played no role in the decision” to keep rates where they are.
Asked about Trump’s recent claims that members of the Fed’s board and rate-setting committee were hostile to the president, Warsh defended his colleagues.

“We just came out of a heck of a family fight, serious, sober discussion,” he said. “I think we came to the right policy decision for this moment, and I’m honored to be here and honored to be the chairman of this group.”
The central bank also acknowledged the economic anxiety gripping much of the country.

“Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace,” the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee said. “While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient.”
Wednesday’s announcement and the Fed’s acknowledgment that inflation remains well above its goal set the stage for a rate increase during December’s monetary policy meeting.

title: Is a water leak detector worth it? Here’s what home experts say
summary: I reached out to home experts to learn more about water leak detectors and exactly how they work. Here’s how you can use them to avoid frozen pipes.
story: With all the content available online these days, it can be hard to figure out what’s real and what’s hype. While we don’t always have the answers, we have a direct line to people who do — which is why we present to you our series The Internet Made Me Ask, where we have experts break down the truth about some of the buzziest trends (and questions) on our timelines, like whether bath sheets are actually different from towels.

It’s expected that homeowners have things like smoke and carbon monoxide detectors in their homes to keep them and their families safe. But another type of home-related detector that’s also worth considering is a water leak detector. Depending on where you live and what type of home you have, a water leak detector can be a very beneficial tool, since it can help track water pressure and temperature, and help you get ahead of frozen pipes in the winter, which can be a major inconvenience — and a costly one if the pipes burst.

To learn more about how water leak detectors actually work and how to shop for one, I spoke to Lou Manfredini, a seasoned home expert at Ace Hardware*, who says that there are several different types of detectors to consider.

While you can technically install it yourself, the brand recommends having a professional do it.
How do water leak detectors work?

Water leak detectors, also sometimes called water leak sensors (which are technically a different type of detector), are systems that monitor water activity in your home. “There are several types, but basically they sense when water is present and will sound an alarm or send you a notification to your phone or computer to alert you of a leak,” says Manfredini. “The basic leak detectors are placed in areas where there may be a concern for water leaking.”

This includes areas like under a sink, under a water heater or in a basement, according to Manfredini. He further explains that they essentially watch for what seems like an excessive use of water, which can sometimes be caused by a burst pipe or a running toilet.

If it’s a point-of-use detector, it can literally sense when water is dripping on it or if it’s pooling around the device on the floor or the surface of a cabinet under a faucet for example. An in-line water detector connects to your pipes to determine changes in flow and temperature (more on this below).
What are the different types of water leak detectors?

There are a few different types of water leak detectors, but in general, you’ll find that many come in one of two forms, according to Chris Petri, owner of Petri Plumbing, Heating, Cooling & Drain Cleaning. These are the types you typically see:

Point-of-use water leak detectors: These types of water leak detectors literally sense water that is flooding around them. They’re commonly placed under a sink or water heater, according to Manfredini, and they will sound an alarm if they come in contact with water droplets or water pooling around them. Brands like Moen and GoveeLife have point-of-use water leak detectors. These types of detectors are usually circular or oblong in shape and adhere to a flat surface under a water source. Some water leak sensors include a power cable you place on the floor that will detect if water has already started to pool around it or if it’s submerged in water. You can use these types of sensors residentially or commercially, according to Manfredini.

Point-of-use water leak detectors: These types of water leak detectors literally sense water that is flooding around them. They’re commonly placed under a sink or water heater, according to Manfredini, and they will sound an alarm if they come in contact with water droplets or water pooling around them. Brands like Moen and GoveeLife have point-of-use water leak detectors. These types of detectors are usually circular or oblong in shape and adhere to a flat surface under a water source. Some water leak sensors include a power cable you place on the floor that will detect if water has already started to pool around it or if it’s submerged in water. You can use these types of sensors residentially or commercially, according to Manfredini.

In-line water leak detectors: “These are installed directly into your water main and use an internal turbine to measure water flow,” says Petri. “The device learns your home’s normal usage patterns—such as flow rate, duration, and volume.” If it detects a change in flow of your water (some also detect change in temperature), it will send you an alert and can automatically shut off the flow of water to prevent any flooding or freezing of pipes. This is also how a water leak detector can help prevent pipes from freezing, since some of them also monitor temperature. What’s also great about these types of detectors is that you don’t actually have to wait for it to start flooding or for it to touch water for it to alert you, according to Petri. The Moen Flo Smart Water Leak Detection Alarm is an example of this type.

This is also how a water leak detector can help prevent pipes from freezing, since some of them also monitor temperature. What’s also great about these types of detectors is that you don’t actually have to wait for it to start flooding or for it to touch water for it to alert you, according to Petri. The Moen Flo Smart Water Leak Detection Alarm is an example of this type.
What should you consider before buying a water leak detector?

“Every home benefits from proactive leak detection,” says Petri. “Waiting until a leak is visually noticeable often means damage has already occurred, especially since leaks frequently happen in hidden areas or while you are away.”

Getting a water leak detector that works for your type of space is important in determining if it’s a worthy investment, so it needs to have certain features. “Key features to consider include automatic water shutoff capabilities, smart notifications (such as app alerts), placement requirements, and whether you need whole-home coverage (in-line) or targeted area protection (point-of-use).”

A step-by-step guide to assembling your charcuterie board
One of the most important considerations when crafting a charcuterie board is how to arrange the foods. Below is a step-by-step guide for the perfect meat and cheese assembly.

Consider what foods you’ll be using. There are several delicious food combinations you can make on a charcuterie board. One thing remains consistent among my experts: it’s the perfect time to work with flavors you love and get creative with other tastes and textures. “When you have something out of the ordinary [on your board], that’s when it becomes a conversation piece. Charcuterie boards actually have a lot of ways of getting people connected,” says Serge Krikorian, owner and head chef of Vibrant Occasions Catering.

Prioritize quality over quantity. “If you take the time to source intentionally, your board will always be delicious,” says Simms, who recommends checking out your local farmers market to find out what is in season near you.

Select a good quality serving board. Choose the right sized board to fit all of your foods without them overflowing, and consider ones with indented edges to catch any loose bites or leftover juices. Some boards might also have specific dips for ramekins or handles so you can take them on the go, experts say.

Determine your arrangement. A basic stack of meats and cheeses won’t be aesthetically pleasing — they need to be assembled the right way. For meats, a salami river and prosciutto ribbons are some of the prettiest and easiest ways to make meat look good, allowing them to flow across or around your board, says Rener. Don’t be afraid to work with different colors and textures, too: red grapes, for example, can make a board look more elevated compared to green grapes, and adding a darker berry, like blackberries, on top can add more height, texture and a contrasting color, according to Rener.

Add bowls and other decorations. To hold loose foods like nuts and olives, consider a ramekin or small bowls for extra flair. Mini dishes are also great for jams and spreads, which not only makes them look good, but keeps them from touching other foods on the board.
Frequently asked questions

Charcuterie is a spread of meats and cheeses typically displayed on a wooden board or a marble or acrylic platter. Traditional charcuterie boards include various types of meats and cheeses, but you may also see crudités boards consisting of vegetables and dips, or dessert boards commonly seen during the holiday season.

“In the food world, we say you eat with your eyes before your mouth, and charcuterie boards really are a great canvas,” says Krikorian. “There’s a lot of great flavors to work with, and so many [opportunities] to make it what you want it to be.”

Though sometimes used interchangeably, there are a few distinct differences between charcuterie and cheese boards. A traditional charcuterie board must include meats (or charcuterie, the French term for a category of prepared meat products from pork, like ham, sausage, pâtés, salami and confit), according to Simms. A cheese board, on the other hand, includes just what its name suggests: a variety of cheeses and other accompaniments like dips and crackers.
“So, if there is no charcuterie involved, it is not considered a charcuterie board,” says Simms.

Charcuterie boards are typically made of wood or marble. Most experts prefer wooden boards for their durability and solid base. Some of them also have handles for practical transport and storage, and side edges to keep treats from falling off, says Rener. Remember that you need to clean and disinfect your board after every use to avoid unappealing smells — you can wash most with soap and water. You’ll also need to condition your wooden board monthly to prevent it from drying out and cracking, says Rener.

Marble boards are another great option because they’re typically scratch-resistant and have a sleek design, making your spread more appealing to guests. Marble is also cooling, so it can keep food fresher for longer compared to wooden boards, experts say.

Simms recommends playing with a variety of textures and flavors, including sweet, salty and crunchy. Typically, charcuterie boards include a mix of meats and cheeses that complement each other, plus a few extras to add texture or sweetness. If you’re a beginner, work with two to four simple varieties of meats and cheeses, like mild salami and Brie, says Cheyenne Nichols, chef and owner of Finest Cravings catering company.

Most experts agree that a charcuterie board will always need some sort of meat. Some of the best ones are prosciutto, coppa, salami and pate, says Simms, who works with cured meat producers like Olympia Provisions, La Quercia, Casella’s, Coro and Fra’mani.

You’ll want to include three to five different cheeses, ideally options that differ in texture (soft or spreadable, semi firm or hard), according to Simms. Your cheese should also vary in milk-type, including cow, goat, sheep and buffalo, she says.

“You’ll want really soft cheese, like a goat cheese or a Brie or Camembert, to serve as the anchor for the board, and then a crumbly cheese of some sort, whether that’s Parmesan or an aged cheddar,” says Rener. Some of my experts’ other favorites are Gouda (soft cheese) and Boursin garlic and herb (spreadable cheese). You may also want to include a “funky” or “stinky” cheese, like blue cheese, to provide a unique taste, says Rener.

Certain cheeses can also add an aesthetic value to your board. “A manchego is great because there are so many different fun ways to slice cheeses like that,” says Rener. She also loves including wine-soaked cheese because the rind adds beauty and texture.
“We love going to our neighborhood cheese shop and getting samples from our local cheesemonger — this is the best way to discover fun, new cheese,” says Simms.

If you want to incorporate fruits, highlight seasonal ones. For example, include peaches if it’s summer, cherries in the spring or pears during winter, according to Rener. There are also a few must-have fruits to include regardless of season: grapes, strawberries, blackberries and raspberries.

Rener also recommends adding two to three types of nuts on your board, including a neutral one like cashews or almonds, and bolder ones like caramelized pecans, spicy pistachios and honey roasted peanuts. “I go crazy for a good candied nut on my charcuterie board,” she says. “Skip the boring nuts and try something new for your board.”

This is where you can add anything your heart desires, primarily if you want additional textures or flavors, or to fill in any gaps. Local honey or honeycomb, seasonal jam and grainy mustard are great spreadables to feature, according to Simms, who also loves pickled cucumbers and olives.

Most people will include jams like a sweet chutney to complement fresher cheeses like manchego, or a savory pepper jam for more buttery cheeses like Brie, says Rener. You can also add crackers, a baguette, crostini and breadsticks for some crunch.

The beauty of a charcuterie board is that you can include whatever type of food you want, and however much you want. But if you’re not sure just how much to add, there are a few parameters to work with, experts say. If you’re going the traditional meat and cheese route, aim for a minimum of two to three ounces of meat and cheese per person for an appetizer portion, and double that amount if you’re not serving other food and it will be more of a meal, says Simms.
My experts suggest working in odd numbers: Choose three or five selections and pick foods diverse in texture (soft, semi firm, hard) and milk-type (cow, goat, sheep).

title: Hayden Panettiere’s death is ruled accidental and police investigation is closed
summary: Panettiere, 36, died of the toxic effects of multiple drugs, including fentanyl, the coroner determined.
story: Actor Hayden Panettiere’s death has been ruled an accident and the case is now closed, police in South Carolina announced Wednesday.

“Based on the Medical Examiner’s determination and the findings of the investigation, Hayden Panettiere’s death has been ruled accidental,” Greenville police said, noting the investigation has concluded.
Panettiere, 36, the actor who starred in the shows “Heroes” and “Nashville,” was found unresponsive on Aug. 16 in a South Carolina apartment complex where she was staying.
Last month, the Greenville County Coroner’s Office ruled her death an accident caused by the toxic effects of multiple drugs: fentanyl, 4-ANPP, alprazolam, methocarbamol and quetiapine.
The coroner said there were no signs of trauma that would have contributed to her death. Police also have said no signs of foul play were found during the initial response and investigation.
Panettiere, who had publicly discussed her struggle with addiction, had been in rehab just weeks before, according to the coroner’s report.

Panettiere’s on-again, off-again boyfriend, Brian Hickerson, was at the apartment complex at the time of her death. He showed police a “bag of medication” he said she was taking at the time, according to the police report.

After the coroner’s report was issued, Panettiere’s mother, Lesley Vogel, called her daughter a “fighter” who was “transparent with her addictions and her numerous rehab attempts show her resolve to live a healthy life.”
Vogel also said at the time that she had “never heard Hayden speak of fentanyl.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

The Drug Enforcement Administration was also investigating, a source familiar with the probe previously told NBC News. The agency typically looks into the narcotics involved in a case, how they were obtained and whether any laws were broken in procuring the drugs.
Panettiere entered Hollywood as a child actor and later carved her own path, starring in the films “Remember the Titans,” “Ice Princess” and “Bring It On: All or Nothing.”

In her memoir, “This Is Me: A Reckoning,” she detailed how her life began to spiral after she had a daughter with Ukrainian heavyweight boxing champion Wladimir Klitschko in 2014. She began drinking heavily to cope with postpartum depression and Klitschko’s distance, she wrote in the book.
She checked into rehab and gave Klitschko custody of their child in 2018.
In the book, she also discussed grappling with pain and grief after her brother, Jansen Panettiere, died in 2023 from an undiagnosed heart condition.

If you or someone you know is struggling with a drug or substance abuse problem, call these numbers for help: The Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration’s national helpline is 1-800-662-HELP (1-800-662-4357); the National Drug Helpline is 1-844-289-0879; and the American Addiction Centers’ hotline is (866) 464-3073.

title: Hasan Piker files $72.5 million defamation suit against Scott Jennings
summary: The progressive pundit claims the conservative commentator deliberately distorted his remarks to falsely portray him as a supporter of lynching Black people.
story: Progressive pundit Hasan Piker has filed a $72.5 million defamation lawsuit against conservative commentator Scott Jennings, claiming Jennings deliberately distorted his remarks to falsely portray him as a supporter of lynching Black people.

Piker, in a 38-page complaint filed Tuesday in federal court in Washington, D.C., said Jennings defamed him on an Aug. 11 episode of “The Scott Jennings Show” when he played video from a 2024 livestream of Piker’s show that had been doctored.

“Mr. Jennings did not merely mischaracterize something Mr. Piker said,” the complaint says. “He took a false, fabricated, and manipulated video of Mr. Piker, added a made-up quotation that Mr. Piker never uttered, and then made accusations that went beyond even what the manipulated footage purported to show.”

Jennings, who is also a CNN commentator, described Piker on the broadcast as a “radical socialist streamer” and Democratic Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed’s “best friend” who has been “calling for Black voters to be lynched.”
“Listen for yourself and understand what the socialists have in store for the black community,” Jennings posted.

“Mr. Piker has never advocated the lynching of Black Americans, or anyone else,” the complaint says. “He has never called for a return to lynchings. And he has never proposed anything remotely resembling the supposed plan that Mr. Jennings falsely attributed to him.”
Jennings did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In the complaint, Piker’s legal team says it sent a written demand to Jennings’ lawyers in August that they issue a retraction. Jennings’ legal team acknowledged it received the letter and said a response would follow, but no “substantive response” has been issued, the complaint says.
As of Wednesday, Jennings’ post including the disputed video was still on X and had racked up 3 million views.

Piker’s legal team also suggests in the complaint that in addition to undermining El-Sayed’s support among Black voters in Michigan, Jennings had a “professional and political incentive” to smear Piker.
“In the weeks surrounding the publications, Mr. Jennings was publicly reported to be under consideration for the position of White House Press Secretary,” the complaint says.

Piker, who is seeking $27.5 million in compensatory damages and $45 million in punitive damages, is a social media maven with more than 3.1 million Twitch followers, 2 million YouTube subscribers and roughly 1.9 million followers on Instagram.
For Subscribers

While Piker has campaigned on behalf of several Democratic candidates, he remains a controversial figure in the party, and several Jewish organizations have accused him of promoting antisemitic tropes and downplaying the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas terrorist attack on Israel.
For Subscribers
In the complaint, Piker alleges that the video Jennings aired combined video from three separate Twitch livestreams and rearranged the sequence of his remarks.
Also, it says, the video shows Piker making sarcastic remarks about going back “to a better time when lynchings were happening.”
But the makers of the video edited out the Oct. 29, 2024, YouTube debate between two Black political commentators — one liberal, the other conservative — that Piker was reacting to.

After a clip of the conservative commentator blaming “woke DAs” for policies that harm Black people ran, the complaint says, Piker responded: “He said, ‘We need more Klansmen, okay? Can we go back to a better time when lynchings were happening? This is what I like as a Black man. Also, there’s no real racism in America.’ My man said, ‘woke DAs,’ dude. What are you saying?”
That clip was taken out of context and presented on Jennings’ show with the caption “PIKER: ‘LET’S GO BACK TO A BETTER TIME WHEN LYNCHINGS WERE HAPPENING,’” which the complaint says Piker never said.
“Mr. Piker was mocking the conservative commentator’s statement,” the complaint says. “Mr. Piker obviously was not expressing support for the Ku Klux Klan, lynching, or racial discrimination.”
Daniel Watkins, an attorney for Piker, told NBC News that what Jennings presented was “a lie.”

“There is something especially disgraceful about exploiting this country’s history of racial terror to destroy another man’s reputation,” Watkins said. “Scott Jennings has every right to disagree with Hasan Piker. He has no right to invent what Hasan said.”

title: Ex-fiancé in ‘The People’s Court’ disappearance charged with murder after phone data review
summary: Dale Smith Jr., of Orlando, Florida, was arrested this month and charged with the second-degree murder of Michelle Parker.
story: A fresh look at cellphone data and text messages led to the arrest of a Florida man accused of murdering his ex-fiancée within hours of taping an episode for “The People’s Court” in 2011, court documents unsealed Tuesday revealed.
Dale Smith Jr., a 55-year-old Orlando resident, was taken into custody Oct. 14 and charged with second-degree murder in the death of Michelle Parker, whose body has never been found, police said.
Smith was 40 and Parker 33 when she was last seen alive on Nov. 17, 2011, the day the episode was taped. The two shared custody of twins at the time.

That afternoon, at about 2 p.m., Parker and Smith appeared for a taping of “The People’s Court” to settle a dispute over a $5,000 engagement ring she allegedly threw off a balcony. The judge ruled “that both parties were responsible for the ring and ordered they split the $5,000.00 damage,” according to an arrest warrant affidavit.
Smith told investigators that, after the taping of the show, Parker dropped the children off at his home and left about 10 minutes later, police said.
But surveillance cameras appeared to show that “the victim’s Hummer was at the suspect’s residence for at least one hour,” according to the affidavit.

Surveillance cameras showed Parker arriving at Smith’s building at about 3:18 p.m., according to the affidavit. At about 4:18 p.m. “victim and suspect phones leaves suspect’s home,” the document said.

By 4:32 p.m., the “victim’s and suspect’s phones continue moving west,” the affidavit said, a route that conflicted with Parker’s plans. “The victim was to travel north to pick up her oldest son who was waiting for her,” it said.

Parker’s brother, Dustin Erickson, also texted her that afternoon asking where she was. Her phone replied, “Waterford,” according to the affidavit. “Waterford” is the common local name for the Waterford Lakes Town Center shopping mall, about 12 miles northeast of Smith’s home.

“The victim’s cell phone never travels east or north towards the Waterford Lakes shopping center,” the affidavit said. “According to Dustin Erickson, the victim had no reason to deceive Dustin as to her location.”

Smith has previously said he had no idea where Parker went after dropping off the children. He told investigators he thought she was “laying low” after the “People’s Court” episode aired, the affidavit said.
“He wanted the victim to come home safe for their kids. However, according to his phone records, he never called or messaged her ever again after November 17, 2011,” the document said.
Police said Smith has a history of domestic violence. Detectives interviewed Jill Van Mechelen, another of his ex-fiancées, whom he knew before he met Parker.

“According to Jill Van Mechelen, the suspect would manually choke (strangle) her during these episodes of domestic physical violence,” the affidavit said. “The suspect also made threats to kill Jill Van Mechelen and her father. Jill Van Mechelen reported that the suspect told her on multiple occasions that he would kill her and/or her father and make them disappear.”
Smith’s attorney declined comment Wednesday, citing a court gag order.

title: Oregon school shooter told police he was assaulted twice in recent years
summary: Police reports describe incidents in recent years in which Griffin John II told police he was punched by a man who had been seeing his mom and hit by his friend’s sister.
story: The 16-year-old boy who killed three children and a teacher, injuring two other people, at a school in Bend, Oregon, was assaulted twice in recent years, once while he was trying to defend his mother, police records show.
In one incident, he told his sister he had been bullied at school, according to police, who wrote that he “likely had a cognitive disability.”
Griffin John II opened fire on a special-needs classroom at Silver Rail Elementary School on Oct. 15 before he was killed by a man who has two daughters at the school.
Much about John remains unknown, and law enforcement is still investigating him and any potential motive. But the police reports show he experienced violence at a young age.

Court and police records previously obtained by NBC News detailed a tumultuous home life, with both parents being involved in violent encounters and run-ins with law enforcement, as well as financial instability.
At age 11, his sister’s friend assaulted him at his home, according to allegations in a Bend police report first obtained by NBC affiliate KGW.

John’s mother, Shauntai Nickerson, told police in the 2022 incident that the friend “slapped John across the face, causing him to chip a tooth,” according to the report. The friend also “punched John in the back of the head,” according to the report.
Nickerson told police that John “had special needs,” and the officer wrote that it appeared he had a cognitive disability, given his “non verbal speech communication and speech patterns.”

John told the officer that after he came home, his sister’s friend asked him whether he wanted to fight and then slapped him, chipping his tooth, according to the report. The officer noticed a small chip on one of John’s lower front teeth, according to the report. John then said the friend “punched him in the back of the head 4 to 6 times,” it said.
John’s sister told the officer that when she got home earlier, John was upset and crying because, he said, he was being bullied at school.
